articles.title: AI data center boom hits growing resistance as $68 billion in US projects are blocked or delayed
articles.text:
A hot potato: Data center developers are facing stronger resistance as they try to add capacity for AI workloads across the United States. The pushback is delaying or blocking projects worth tens of billions of dollars and prompting states and local governments to scrutinize their power, water and land-use demands. As the AI buildout accelerates, community opposition is becoming a material obstacle to the industry's ability to add computing capacity at the pace it wants.
Local opposition blocked or delayed 45 data center projects valued at $68 billion during the second quarter, according to Data Center Watch, a research initiative from AI intelligence company 10a Labs. The affected projects accounted for more than half of the large-scale data center developments the group began tracking during the period.
The disputes are centered on the practical demands of AI infrastructure. New facilities require large amounts of electricity, water and land, and often need new transmission lines, substations or other utility upgrades. In some areas, residents are challenging individual projects. Elsewhere, local governments are considering moratoriums or new rules before developers submit permit applications.
Data Center Watch said it identified 843 groups opposing data center development in 49 states. Hawaii was the only state without a group on its list. The organization also said 30 statehouses introduced or adopted measures related to data center siting, electricity use or water consumption.
"New groups continue to emerge, opposition is appearing across a wide range of states and jurisdictions, and online petition signatures continue to grow," Miquel Vila, the group's lead analyst, told Bloomberg.
The second-quarter total was below the first quarter, when Data Center Watch counted 75 contested projects with an estimated value of about $130 billion. But the latest figures show that resistance is affecting a large share of proposed developments, not just a few high-profile projects.
For the technology industry, the issue is becoming a constraint on AI expansion. Companies including Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Alphabet are building more and more data centers to support training and inference workloads, which require significant amounts of electricity and cooling.
Developers have pursued several approaches to meet those needs, including larger grid connections, dedicated generation and on-site power systems. Those plans can create additional opposition, especially when they involve natural gas generation or major utility infrastructure.
Water use is another concern. Operators have promoted cooling systems designed to reduce consumption, including closed-loop designs. Critics, however, argue that even more efficient systems can place pressure on local supplies when deployed at the scale required for major AI campuses.
Opposition has also spread through online campaigns. One petition against a proposed Tennessee project drew more than 500,000 signatures on Change.org during the quarter, Data Center Watch said. The group said the petition represented more than one-third of all signatures collected on the platform during that period.
Data Center Watch is also seeing similar campaigns outside the United States. The group expanded its reporting this year to include opposition in Europe, Australia, South Africa and other regions. Those efforts focus on many of the same issues seen in the US, including project approvals, power demand and water use.
"As with many other trends, the US has generally been at the forefront, but the phenomenon is increasingly becoming global," Vila said. "We anticipate that this will just become more prominent as data center development expands across the globe."

articles.title: Lawsuit demands OpenAI pay for new school after ChatGPT used in shooting
articles.text:
Two police officers leave Tumbler Ridge Secondary school two days after the rural community experienced one of Canada's deadliest shootings in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia.
Credit:
PAIGE TAYLOR WHITE / Contributor | AFP
Two police officers leave Tumbler Ridge Secondary school two days after the rural community experienced one of Canada's deadliest shootings in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia.
Credit:
PAIGE TAYLOR WHITE / Contributor | AFP
The families of victims killed in one of the deadliest mass shootings in Canada’s history have already sued OpenAI over its failure to warn law enforcement after discovering in advance that the shooter was using ChatGPT to plan the violence.
Now, British Columbia is suing, explaining for the first time how costly and extreme the disaster response has been. OpenAI and Sam Altman owe the tiny remote mining community shattered by the tragedy much more than an apology, the Canadian province argued. They must make meaningful changes to end ChatGPT-assisted violence and then pay whatever it costs to help Tumbler Ridge to rebuild, recover, and heal.
In a complaint filed Monday, British Columbia explained that Tumbler Ridge Secondary School had to be demolished after an 18-year-old transgender shooter, Jesse Van Rootselaar, died by suicide there in February after killing five kids and an education assistant. In total, eight lives were lost, as prior to the school shooting, Van Rootselaar shot their mother and half-brother.
Previously, the secondary school sat “in the heart of the town, both geographically and culturally,” the lawsuit said. But after the shooting, it became an unavoidable “symbol of the trauma.”
About 160 students, teachers, and staff “were trapped in classrooms and closets” at the school for hours, and they were too traumatized to ever go back. To provide “at least some small relief to those who have suffered the most intensely,” demolition began in August, and the community hopes to have a replacement school built at a new location by the end of this year, if all goes to plan.
British Columbia argued that OpenAI and Altman should pay for the school, as well as cover a wide range of other emergency costs that never would have been incurred if not for “this tragedy and its foreseeable consequences.” They also asked the court to provide injunctive relief, including requiring OpenAI to update ChatGPT to automatically terminate violent conversations.
BC wants to see the ChatGPT logs
Most urgently, British Columbia and the local school district’s Board of Education have asked the court for an immediate order that would force OpenAI to share Van Rootselaar’s chat logs with the public for the first time.
So far, OpenAI has only shared the logs with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP). Asked for comment on whether there’s any plan to release the chat logs to the public—as a Florida law enforcement agency did following a prior ChatGPT-linked shooting at Florida State University—RCMP declined to comment. Instead, they pointed Ars to a July statement, where the RCMP would only confirm that police are reviewing information from online accounts. In a seeming acknowledgment that the public wants answers, the statement also offered a reminder that “it is important to understand that the absence of publicly disclosed details does not mean investigators do not have that information.”
OpenAI declined to comment directly on the lawsuit or requested remedies. The company has said that it was protecting Van Rootselaar’s privacy when the decision was made to override human review teams recommending that the violent chat logs be shared with police. Today, a spokesperson told Ars that “what happened in Tumbler Ridge was an unspeakable tragedy, and our thoughts remain with the victims, their families, and the entire community. OpenAI remains committed to working collaboratively with government and law enforcement officials, and continuing to advance our ongoing safety work.”
British Columbia maintains that OpenAI has not made ChatGPT any safer following several mass shootings that established “recurring” patterns of violent ChatGPT use. Further, the firm’s rationale for ignoring the threat seemed untrustworthy. British Columbia suspects that OpenAI actually wanted to avoid drawing a hard line that would require OpenAI to report more violent users to the police and expose the public to more of the real-world threats that chatbots could pose. The province accused OpenAI of hiding the chat logs to protect its potentially $1 trillion IPO.
To British Columbia, it seems like OpenAI is doing little to combat the most violent threats. Their complaint noted that OpenAI claimed it made an “attempt” to block violent chats in December 2025, but that change did not stop Van Rootselaar’s harmful use during that time or any time in the months after. At a press conference covered by The Wall Street Journal, British Columbia’s attorney general, Niki Sharma, said that “we should be asking them why” they won’t release the chat logs.
“In any other circumstance where a person aids, encourages or conspires to commit a criminal oﬀense or is criminally negligent, they can be investigated, prosecuted, and judged,” Sharma said. “There is no AI exemption to those criminal law principles.”
“We all know the victims”
The shooting on February 10, 2026, left everyone in Tumbler Ridge reeling. The population is only 2,700. A local official summed up the extent of the crisis by saying, “We all know the victims.”
Tumbler Ridge Secondary School closed the day of the shooting and never reopened. For the kids recovering and seeking normalcy, that has been a problem, since there is no other school in the town. Instead, they’ve been attending a temporary school on a makeshift campus “assembled first from fourteen Ministry of Forestry trailers,” then eventually converted into “larger modular classrooms.”
Throwing together a functioning school on the fly wasn’t cheap or easy, the school district said in the complaint. They had to “furnish it, recruit and train replacement educators for local staff who could not return, and reorganize instruction around the absence of murdered students and colleagues.”
As for the old school, it cost money to demolish it, and none of these emergency resources are considered “recurring public services that governments fund through taxation and spread across all taxpayers,” the complaint said.
In addition to the school, they’re also building a wellness center, as demand for counseling has not gone down since the tragedy. Acute and ongoing health care, victim services, and trauma-informed mental health care are all considered necessary services the community will need for years to come. As the complaint emphasized, OpenAI should have deliberately considered how small the community was when weighing the threat the shooter posed:
Unlike other larger communities, in Tumbler Ridge there were no redundancies of personnel or facilities to carry the community following the tragedy. There was no other school building to house students for education or counseling following this trauma. There were few available adults to step in for teachers and administrators who were directly impacted by the assault. Students, parents and all those impacted needed immediate support and counseling, and there simply were not enough people in this small town to match the need.
There were also “no substitute teachers, no standby clinicians, and no extra police officers,” the complaint alleged, and what front-line workers were available “were themselves traumatized.” To help, British Columbia transported in temporary workers, who needed temporary housing, to keep up with demand for emergency services.
In the three months following the shooting, “Child & Youth Mental Health alone delivered well over 900 counseling sessions to more than 100 unique children and families, and Northern Health treated more than 130 unique adults,” the lawsuit reported. More recently, British Columbia has started shifting from offering an emergency response to supporting long-term recovery, including establishing a long-term grief-and-bereavement working group. Those solutions will require substantial investments.
On top of that, British Columbia and the school district have also paid for an “extraordinary policing response.” That’s still necessary, they argued, since the community worries that potential copycat shooters pose a real threat. The complaint alleged that RCMP has already investigated copycat threats.
“Demand for scheduled mental-health services remains high and spikes around anniversary dates and other triggering events; these services are expected to be needed for years to come,” the lawsuit said.
ChatGPT “reinforced” violent ideation
OpenAI first detected the violent chats in June 2025. At that time, human reviewers “examined the flagged conversations” and “concluded that the shooter presented a credible and specific risk of gun violence to real people,” whistleblowers told the WSJ. Disagreeing, however, OpenAI leadership intervened to block reports to law enforcement, overruling their own safety teams and claiming that “the matter did not satisfy a ‘higher threshold’ for ‘credible and imminent’ threat reporting.”
Ultimately, instead of reporting the user to RCMP or warning the community, OpenAI simply deactivated the account, which did nothing to prevent Van Rootselaar from making a second account.
At that time, OpenAI was publicly claiming that any violent conversations would be reviewed by humans and reported to law enforcement to deter real-world tragedies. ChatGPT had been linked to the FSU shooting, as well as to a Cybertruck bombing in Las Vegas, and British Columbia alleged that the Tumbler Ridge shooter should’ve been flagged as threatening as the users in those cases.
After the whistleblowers outed OpenAI for failing to warn authorities, OpenAI claimed that it “was reluctant to make such referrals because they would require it to disclose how its product contributes to the threat environment.” But that didn’t ring true to British Columbia and the Tumbler Ridge community. They think it seemed like OpenAI was hoping that empty promises to do better would protect “its valuation, and its anticipated public offering.” In Tumbler Ridge, the youngest victims who actually needed protecting were 12 and 13, they noted.
The complaint suggested that OpenAI’s defense will likely be to blame Van Rootselaar for their violent inputs, while downplaying ChatGPT’s outputs.
But even without the logs, British Columbia alleged that the defect with ChatGPT is not its users, but its design. Allegedly, OpenAI turned off functionality that would have terminated the Tumbler Ridge chats, then introduced a more sycophantic model that it already knew had assisted users bent on causing real-world violence. Since ChatGPT’s release, the model spec has always instructed the chatbot to assume “good faith” and “not to probe intent” when users initiated violent chats, and British Columbia wants the court to order those two instructions specifically to be changed.
Still, the community wants to see the chat logs, and so does British Columbia, which is funding their recovery.
The province alleged that the ChatGPT logs will show that OpenAI’s product dangerously “facilitated the mental instability of the shooter” by encouraging, elaborating, and reinforcing violent ideation “instead of interrupting it or directing the user to real-world help.”
In a loss, OpenAI could face extensive damages, including an order to cover the costs of emergency responses. They could also face punitive damages if the failure to warn police is deemed willful.
OpenAI “repeatedly represented to users and the public that it detected users who present a risk of harm to others, routed such conversations to trained reviewers authorized to act, and referred imminent threats of serious physical harm to law enforcement,” the complaint said. “Having held itself out as voluntarily undertaking and performing exactly the protective function” that a law imposing a duty to warn requires, “OpenAI cannot disclaim the duty it publicly assumed,” the lawsuit said.
Altman’s apology is not enough
In April 2026, Altman publicly acknowledged that OpenAI failed the Tumbler Ridge community.
“I am deeply sorry that we did not alert law enforcement to the account that was banned in June,” Altman said.
According to British Columbia, the account was never banned, and that apology is “an admission” that “OpenAI did not notify law enforcement after its safety team identified the risk of violence.”
To ensure the most violent chats are always routed to police, the province asked the court to order OpenAI to conduct regular independent audits.
The company’s conduct “was despicable,” the lawsuit said.
“Had OpenAI implemented a meaningful user ban,” the shooter would not have had continued access to ChatGPT, which allegedly “increased the shooter’s lethality.” And had OpenAI reported the user to law enforcement, any weapons the shooter used could have been removed from the house, as the shooter was already on the local law authorities’ radar, the lawsuit alleged.
Ashley is a senior policy reporter for Ars Technica, dedicated to tracking social impacts of emerging policies and new technologies. She is a Chicago-based journalist with 20 years of experience.

articles.title: Glorious GMMK Eternal Review: Fits anywhere, sounds great
articles.text:
Tom's Hardware Verdict
The GMMK Eternal isn't the most exciting keyboard, but it sounds good and takes up very little space.
Pros
- +Compact size that's not overly cramped
- +Excellent sound-damping
- +$100
Cons
- -OEM profile keycaps
- -Generic-looking
- -ABS keycaps in OEM profile
Why you can trust Tom's Hardware
Something, something, going back to your roots. I guess that's what Glorious is doing (or, thinks it's doing) with the GMMK Eternal — its new wired mechanical gaming keyboard.
The GMMK Eternal is, at a glance, pretty basic: it's wired, it has regular mechanical (not magnetic) switches and a standard 1,000 Hz polling rate. It comes with bright backlighting, double-shot ABS keycaps, and some gamer-friendly features such as multiple onboard profiles and macro-recording via Glorious Core. It also has a hot-swappable PCB and three layers of sound-dampening material in the case — it's not supposed to be a revolution, but it is a pretty solid option if you're looking for something compact and relatively budget-friendly. The GMMK Eternal is available now in black, with GMMK's Fox MX linear switches, for $99.99.
Design and Construction of the GMMK Eternal
The GMMK Eternal is a wired mechanical gaming keyboard with a compact 96-percent layout — it has a full function row, arrow keys, and a 10-key numberpad, but everything is squashed together (and it ditches most of the navigation keys), so it takes up significantly less space than a full-size keyboard but has almost as many keys. It sports a fairly simple, minimalist overall design — edge-to-edge keys with virtually no bezel, black anodized aluminum top plate over a black ABS plastic bottom case, and no obvious branding on the top or sides.
The keyboard measures approximately 14.6 inches (372mm) wide by 4.8 inches (122mm) deep, and is 1.7 inches (44mm) thick at its thickest point (including the keycaps). That's significantly smaller than a full-size keyboard, and is even small by 96-percent keyboard standards — perhaps my favorite 96-percent keyboard, the Asus ROG Strix Scope II 96 Wireless, is slightly larger than the GMMK Eternal at 14.84 x 5.16 inches (377 x 131mm), though at 1.57 inches (40mm) thick, it's slightly lower-profile. This is because the GMMK Eternal has double-shot ABS keycaps with shine-through legends in an OEM profile (the ROG Strix Scope II 96 Wireless comes with keycaps in a mid-height profile that's very close to the Cherry profile).
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
While the GMMK Eternal is pretty compact, even by 96-percent keyboard standards, you won't feel too cramped for space. There's enough room to leave some separation between the alphanumeric keys and the arrow keys (though not much), and there's enough room in the top row that the Function keys are grouped into visibly distinct groups of four. There are five navigation keys next to the Function row and above the numberpad: PrintScreen, Delete, Insert, Page Up, and Page Down. So you really shouldn't miss too much about your full-size board once you get used to the numberpad being right on top of you.
The GMMK Eternal has some weight to it, but it's not too hefty: it weighs in at just under two pounds (1.94 lbs / 879 g), which is about what we'd expect for a board of this size and construction. For comparison, the wired Corsair Vanguard Pro 96 weighs about 2.2 pounds (998g), while the wireless Asus ROG Strix Morph 96 Wireless weighs just under 2.5 pounds (2.48 lbs / 1,125 g). The GMMK Eternal is heavy enough that it shouldn't move around on your desk too much during heavy gaming sessions, but it's not so heavy that it would be difficult to travel with.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
The bottom of the keyboard is where you'll finally see Glorious' branding. The Glorious name is stamped across the back, debossed with a shiny finish. There are also a couple strips of anti-slip rubber, as well as two sets of plastic flip-out feet for adjusting the keyboard's angle. The GMMK Eternal is a wired keyboard, and it has one USB-C port in the center of the board.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
The GMMK Eternal comes with just two accessories in the box: a 6-foot (1.8m) rubber-coated USB-C to USB-A cable and a 2-in-1 combination keycap and switch puller.
Specs
| Size | 96% | 
| Number of keys | 99 | 
| Switches | Glorious Fox Switches | 
| Backlighting | Yes | 
| Onboard Storage | Yes (3 profiles) | 
| Dedicated Media Keys | No | 
| Game Mode | Yes / No | 
| Additional Ports | 0 | 
| Connectivity | Wired (USB-C) | 
| Cable | 6ft. / 1.8m USB-C to USB-A | 
| Keycaps | double-shot ABS | 
| Construction | Anodized aluminum top plate ABS bottom case | 
| Software | Glorious Core | 
| Dimensions (LxWxH) | 14.6 x 4.8 x 1.7" / 372 x 122 x 44mm | 
| Weight | 1.94lbs / 879g | 
| MSRP / Price at Time of Review | $99.99 | 
| Release Date | Sept. 8, 2026 | 
Typing and Gaming Experience on the GMMK Eternal
The GMMK Eternal is a mechanical gaming keyboard with a hot-swappable PCB that takes both 3- and 5-pin switches. It comes pre-built with Glorious' Fox switches, which are pre-lubed linear switches with an actuation force of 55g — a little heavier than your average linear switch, but I kind of liked the extra force. The switches are otherwise typical linear switches, with smooth, stable keypresses that have no tactile bump or audible click. They're rated for 50 million clicks.
The keyboard features three layers of sound-dampening material in the case: a molded silicone layer and two layers of PU foam around the PCB, for a "deeper, more satisfying thock." And I'll admit that I was pretty impressed with how the GMMK Eternal sounded out of the box — especially for a sub-$100 keyboard from a mainstream gaming company. There was a small amount of rattle as I typed, but the case, at least, was solid and ping-less, and bottoming out did give a deeper sound (if not quite a "thock").
The GMMK Eternal comes with double-shot ABS keycaps in an OEM profile, which is the standard, medium-height profile you'll find on most mainstream gaming keyboards. The keycaps have lightly cupped, textured tops with shine-through legends and secondary legends printed on the sides in white. While I usually prefer lower-profile keycaps, I didn't mind these — the keyboard is fairly compact and low-profile to begin with, so I didn't find the standard height OEM profile to be uncomfortable (nor did I feel like I needed a wrist rest).
The GMMK Eternal is a solid option for both typing and gaming — I didn't have any issues with accuracy, speed, or response time in my testing, minus the normal learning curve of getting used to having the arrow keys right on top of the alphanumeric keys.
Features and Software of the GMMK Eternal
The GMMK Eternal is configurable with Glorious' universal peripheral software, Glorious Core, which I don't have any real problems with, save for the fact that it requires a restart upon install. The keyboard has onboard storage, and you can set up up to three profiles in Glorious Core to save directly to the hardware.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
You can use Glorious Core to adjust the keyboard's settings, including polling rate, input latency, and lighting standby timer, as well as switching between Windows and Mac modes. This isn't a magnetic switch keyboard, so there's not much else to set up in terms of performance. You can also remap keys — up to two layers deep, and the software has a built-in macro recorder and manager.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
You can also customize the keyboard's lighting, which looks great — the board features bright RGB backlighting with a north-facing PCB, and the board's otherwise boring design really lets the lighting shine. There are 17 different lighting presets in Glorious Core, and you can also customize the lighting for each key individually (if you want).
The Bottom Line
The Glorious GMMK Eternal isn't the most exciting keyboard on the market, especially not for gaming. It's a wired keyboard with mechanical switches and a standard 1,000 Hz polling rate, so it's not trying to be the fastest, lowest-latency, RapidTrigger-enabled keyboard that will launch you into a pro-eSports career. Instead, it's a simple, compact keyboard that offers a very solid typing and gaming experience with hot-swappable switches and pretty RGB lighting for the relatively budget-friendly price of $100. While you can definitely find keyboards for less than $100, you probably won't find one that sounds and feels better than the GMMK Eternal.
Sarah Jacobsson Purewal is a senior editor at Tom's Hardware covering peripherals, software, and custom builds. You can find more of her work in PCWorld, Macworld, TechHive, CNET, Gizmodo, Tom's Guide, PC Gamer, Men's Health, Men's Fitness, SHAPE, Cosmopolitan, and just about everywhere else.

articles.title: ‘Hi, it’s AI speaking’: Base44 just launched AI that can handle phone calls
articles.text:
‘Hi, it’s AI speaking’: Base44 just launched AI that can handle phone calls
Would you pick up?
- Base44 has launched an AI agent that can make and receive phone calls
- It aims to eliminate hold times and speed up research
- Just describe your goal, give context, and let it do the work for you
Waiting on hold may become a thing of the past thanks to Base44’s new voice AI agent. Launched earlier this month, Superagent can now make and receive phone calls on behalf of the user, with countless potential applications.
According to a press release shared with TechRadar Pro, Base44’s Superagent can take on everyday tasks that would otherwise require people to spend time on hold or leave them navigating frustrating phone systems.
How Base 44’s Superagent works
Users start by giving Superagent a goal and providing relevant context on how that goal should be achieved. The AI agent can then proactively contact businesses or customers, asking relevant questions, collecting crucial information, and even navigating supported phone menus. Once the job is complete, the agent will then report back to the user with a summary of what has been done and which outcomes have been achieved.
Some helpful use cases include:
- Improve time management by booking or rescheduling important appointments
- Speed up research by calling vendors to request quotes for comparison
- Increase call success by retrying unanswered calls on a predefined schedule
- Receive and manage calls from trusted contacts
A shifting approach to AI
The launch highlights an ongoing shift in consumer AI, with tools moving from generative AI that simply answers questions to agentic AI that undertakes real-world actions based on requests made by the user.
But the question remains: will humans be happy to interact with AI if it means limiting wait times and more efficient calls?

Sua tela AMOLED Dinâmico 2X de 6,9″ possui taxa de 120 Hz e brilho de até 2.600 nits, combinação capaz de reproduzir imagens com cores vibrantes e alta fluidez nas transições em apps e games, além de ter visibilidade garantida em qualquer ambiente.
O kit principal de câmeras filma em 8K. Ele é formado por uma wide de 200 MP com OIS e uma ultrawide de 50 MP, que captam belas cenas ao ar livre, uma telefoto de 10 MP com zoom óptico de 3x e uma periscópica de 50 MP e 5x para aproximações com qualidade. A frontal de 12 MP filma em 4K a 60 fps e tira ótimas selfies.
O corpo de titânio do S25 Ultra é revestido de ambos os lados pelo vidro Gorilla Armor 2, resistente contra riscos e arranhões, enquanto a certificação IP68 confere proteção em cenários como poeira intensa e mergulhos acidentais.
Sua bateria de 5.000 mAh resiste a até 31 horas de reprodução de vídeo, segundo a Samsung. O suporte ao carregamento rápido de 45 W via USB-C e de 15 W sem fio permite o uso prolongado por um dia inteiro, recurso essencial para usuários com agendas corridas.
O Galaxy S25 Ultra de 256 GB (R$ 5.099 no Pix com cupom INFLU300) será atualizado até o Android 22 e conversa com redes 5G, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 5.4 e NFC.

articles.title: Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 : pourquoi Qualcomm lance deux puces pour vos futurs smartphones
articles.text:
Deux processeurs pour le prix d’un : rompant avec sa tradition, Qualcomm annonce aujourd’hui non pas une, mais deux puces haut de gamme pour les smartphones Android les plus chers de l’année prochaine.
En lieu et place d’un unique Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 pour succéder au précédent SD 8 Elite Gen 5, l’entreprise a développé en parallèle une seconde puce appelée Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 – tout est donc la mention « Extreme ». Une mention qui sera votre point de vigilance dans les mois qui viennent pour identifier la meilleure des deux puces.
Qualcomm justifie ainsi la décision de lancer deux puces haut de gamme : « Le marché des smartphones a changé et Qualcomm s’adapte », a expliqué sur scène Chris Patrick, vice-président sénior et responsable général de la division mobile de Qualcomm. « Entre les terminaux pliants, ceux dédiés au gaming ou à la photo, nos clients cherchent à se différencier et ont besoin de puces différentiées pour cela », a-t-il assuré.
Quant à la différentiation justement, Qualcomm ne l’a pas rendue bien aisée : la seule différence entre les deux logos tient dans le cadre extérieur doré, plus large dans le cas de la version Extreme. Pas de gros « X » facilement identifiable, pas de changement de teinte/couleur, etc. Si nous hésitions entre timidité excessive (volontaire ou non) ou ratée de communication, la réalité pour Chris Patrick est que « nous voulons que les consommateurs cherchent uniquement la mention Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6. C’est aux constructeurs de choisir la bonne puce pour les bons usages ».
Qualcomm rejoint le club des 2 nm
Avant de parler de détails architecturaux, parlons finesse de gravure : cette sixième génération est la première de l’histoire de Qualcomm à utiliser le nœud TSMC N2, abusivement appelé 2 nanomètres. Après trois générations en 4 nm, puis deux en 3 nm, on sent l’accélération reprendre en matière de finesse de gravure !
Après l’Exynos 2600 de Samsung lancé en début d’année (qui ne réussit pas à la version européenne du Galaxy S26…), conçu autour de la gravure maison du coréen (SF2), après leA20 Pro d’il y a 15 jours (et le M6 du mois dernier), ou encore le MediaTek Dimensity 9600 Pro de la semaine dernière, Qualcomm est donc le dernier larron à dévoiler les détails de ses puces gravées en 2 nm. Comme à l’accoutumée, ce sont donc les grands volumes (et donc les petites puces) du marché des smartphones qui profitent les premières de la finesse la plus à la pointe de l’industrie.
Mais comme vous allez le voir, si cette plus grande finesse de gravure permet d’ajouter quelques transistors en plus et de pousser un peu plus loin les fréquences, le vrai bénéfice de cette transition est à chercher du côté de l’énergie.
CPU : le premier cœur mobile à 5 GHz
Commençons par le bloc CPU, le processeur qui fait tourner Android. Du point de vue architectural, on reste sur la famille de cœurs Oryon maison, conçue par le père des CPU Apple, qui passent pour l’occasion en génération 4 – mais nous n’avons pas plus de précisions pour le moment. L’organisation ne bouge pas : deux « Prime Cores », les brutes de calcul, et six « Performance Cores ». Huit cœurs au total épaulés par 16 Mo de cache baptisé Oryon Flex Cache.
La course à la puissance continue et, fait historique sur mobile, les cœurs Prime atteignent, la fréquence record de 5 GHz (4,6 GHz l’an dernier) ! Les six autres profitent eux aussi d’un boost de puissance et passent de 3,6 GHz à 4 GHz. De quoi permettre à Qualcomm de revendiquer le titre de « CPU mobile le plus rapide au monde ». Mais il faut ici prendre la rapidité au sens fréquence et non performance pure : les mesures de performances parleront quand les terminaux seront dans nos mains.
Ces gains de fréquences se traduisent par des gains de performance, mais qui semblent plus modestes que l’an dernier : +13 % pour l’Extreme et +10 % pour le 8 Elite Gen 6, quand le Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 revendiquait +20 % à finesse de gravure égale. Ces gains suivent de près la hausse des fréquences, ce qui laisse penser que l’architecture a peu bougé cette année.
L’efficacité énergétique progresse en revanche de 37 % sur les deux puces, marque qu’il s’agit là du principal bénéfice du passage au 2 nm. Notez que nous poserons la question aux ingénieurs sur place. Reste une inconnue de taille : les deux fiches techniques décrivent un CPU strictement identique, en nature comme en fréquences, pour des gains de performance différents : d’où vient le delta ? Nous poserons les questions aux ingénieurs, mais cela ne devrait pas venir de l’interface mémoire, les deux puces gérant aussi bien la LPDDR5X que la nouvelle comme la LPDDR6 (jusqu’à 24 Go).
iPhone 18 Pro à 99€ + forfait 250Go à 29,99€/mois pendant 12 mois. Profitez de 50€ de remise immédiate avec le code NEW50 et jusqu’à 150€ de bonus reprise pour votre ancien mobile. Livraison offerte.
GPU : des cœurs dédiés à l’IA, mais pas pour tout le monde
C’est sur la partie graphique que l’écart se creuse le plus : +44 % de performances annoncées pour l’Extreme, +35 % pour le 8 Elite Gen 6, avec dans les deux cas 40 % d’efficacité énergétique en plus. Le GPU Adreno – toujours sans numéro de série, ce qui n’aide pas à s’y retrouver – conserve son architecture en trois blocs (appelées slices, ou tranches en anglais), désormais cadencés à 1,45 GHz sur l’Extreme contre 1,2 GHz l’an dernier.
Comme pour le précédent SD 8 Elite Gen 5, le nouveau GPU classique profite d’une mémoire interne de 18 Mo. L’intégration de cette mémoire hautes performances (HPM) évite une partie des allers-retours vers la mémoire vive, des opérations particulièrement énergivores. Elle reste à 18 Mo sur l’Extreme, avec une architecture revue à laquelle Qualcomm attribue 12 % d’économies d’énergie.
La vraie nouveauté est réservée à la version extrême et s’appelle Adreno Neural Fusion. Si vous êtes gamer, le principe de cette technologie rappelle le DLSS de Nvidia : un mélange de super résolution couplée à de la génération d’images. En clair : la puce calcule la scène dans une petite définition et augmenter la résolution via l’IA, puis d’autres algorithmes IA inventent des trames interstitielles pour augmenter le nombre d’images par seconde.
L’Adreno Neural Fusion s’appuie sur des cœurs matriciels implantés au sein même du GPU. Et en marge de l’amélioration des performances, Qualcomm annonce jusqu’à 40 % d’économies d’énergie – sur une démo maison, précisons-le. La technologie est déjà intégrée aux moteurs Unreal Engine, Unity et Messiah, et une vingtaine de jeux sont annoncés compatibles.
NPU : de plus gros modèles et l’accélération des agents
Le processeur neuronal dévolu aux calculs d’IA, appelé NPU (neural processing unit) est lui aussi profondément remanié. Il s’organise désormais en 12 unités scalaires, 8 vectorielles, une tensorielle et un nouveau bloc appelé Element Accelerator. Cette nouvelle brique technologique a été créée pour accélérer les actions des agents IA.
Concrètement, l’Element Accelerator évite aux agents de repartir de zéro à chaque nouvelle étape de calcul, avec une limite de contexte allant jusqu’à 32 000 jetons (tokens). Autre nouveauté, la prise en charge de la précision INT2, un niveau de précision inférieur qui permet de faire tenir de gros modèles de plusieurs dizaines de milliards de paramètres dans un smartphone.
Grâce à un supplément de +50% de mémoire partagée en plus et une configuration améliorée, seul le SD 8 Elite Extreme est à même d’exécuter de manière locale les modèles appelés « Mixture of Experts » (MoE). Ces modèles, pris en charge jusqu’à 30 milliards de paramètres, sont très importants : comme seulement une fraction des agents « experts » s’active à chaque requête, cela les rend, là encore, exploitables sur smartphone.
Les deux puces partagent cependant le même Sensing Hub, ce coprocesseur basse consommation toujours éveillée qui est, responsable, par exemple, du pilotage à la voix du type « OK Google ». Toujours taillée pour ne consommer que quelques milliwatts, cette petite puce dans la puce passe à deux micro-NPU pour proposer 85 % de performances en plus. Il peut faire tourner en permanence des modèles de 200 millions de paramètres et s’avère responsable d’alimenter Personal Scribe.
Présenté sous forme théorique au MWC en février 2025, cette une fonction apprend de vos messages, de vos courriels et de vos conversations pour bâtir votre « graphe de connaissances » personnel (personal graph). L’intérêt principal de ce personal graph est son exécution locale, que Qualcomm présente comme un argument majeur en termes de confidentialité. Mais Qualcomm reste toujours un peu vague quant aux apps qui l’intègreront.
Photo et vidéo : la 8K60 réservée à l’Extreme
L’an dernier, l’ISP (image signal processor, en charge du traitement de l’image) du SD 8 ELite Gen 5 était le premier à intégrer un circuit entièrement dédié à la vidéo computationnelle. Cette année, le socle commun des deux nouvelles puces reprend ses trois processeurs d’image 20 bits et ses capteurs jusqu’à 320 mégapixels. Mais Qualcomm a ajouté trois nouvelles briques : l’Intelligent Pixel Control, qui associe 16 bits de données d’IA à chaque pixel pour mieux comprendre la scène, l’Elite Color Engine, qui applique en temps réel des tables de conversion colorimétrique (3D LUT), et le Motion Intelligence, qui anticipe les mouvements pour stabiliser l’image.
C’est du côté de la vidéo que la puce Extreme marque le plus sa différence en matière d’image : si le SD 8 Elite Gen 6 filme bien en 8K30p, l’Extreme est le seul à proposer non seulement la 8K60p, mais aussi les ralentis 4K240p (ralenti x8) images par seconde, quand le 8 Elite Gen 6 plafonne respectivement à 30 et 120 images par seconde.
Du côté de la vidéo, si la génération précédente accueillait un codec haute qualité – l’APV, un concurrent du ProRES d’Apple – cette nouvelle fournée de puces intègre un nouveau codec haute compression appelé VVC ou H.266. Successeur du HEVC/H.265, ce Versatile Video Coding codec a une promesse majeure : réduire le débit de 30 % à 50 % par rapport au H265 à qualité visuelle égale. Un codec que beaucoup estiment obligatoire pour faciliter la diffusion des flux 4K et 8K les plus exigeants.
5G de pointe et début du Wi-Fi 8
Souvent ignoré, le modem est pourtant une pièce maîtresse des system on a chip (SoC) pour smartphones – si vous en doutez, pourquoi diable Apple a mis plusieurs années à développer ses C1 et C2 ! Après le X85 du SD 8 Elite Gen 5, cette fournée de Gen 6 reçoit le modem X105.
Ce modem est le premier de l’histoire à se conformer à la dernière norme 5G, la Release 19 du 3GPP (qui sera l’une des dernières marches de la 5G Advanced avant l’arrivée de la 6G). Les débits maximaux théoriques grimpent à 14,8 Gbit/s en téléchargement et 4,2 Gbit/s en envoi, contre 12,5 et 3,7 Gbit/s auparavant. Comme l’an dernier, autant prévenir : à moins de vivre sous une antenne, personne ne verra jamais ces chiffres. Le bénéfice réel se détectera sans doute plutôt dans la stabilité de la connexion.
Et on reste dans le domaine de la stabilité avec le nouveau module FastConnect 8800, qui prend en charge, pour la première fois, le Wi-Fi 8. Cette nouvelle norme appelée 802.11bn, est la première à délaisser la course à la vitesse pure pour se concentrer sur la stabilité et la réduction de la latence, une ambition réunie sous la bannière de l’ultra-haute fiabilité (UHR).
Mais si l’organe de standardisation du Wi-Fi 8 communique plus volontiers sur la recherche de robustesse et de stabilité de cette nouvelle norme, cela n’empêche pas les ingénieurs de Qualcomm de tenter de repousser les limites. Ainsi, dans une configuration d’antenne 4×4 (quatre antennes en émission, quatre en réception), inédite sur smartphone, ce module promet un débit de pointe de 11,6 Gbit/s. Attention cependant : a prise en charge du Wi-Fi 8 ne concernera que certaines versions d’Android. Il faut en effet des antennes spéciales pour activer les technologies comme l’UHR.
Xiaomi et Lenovo dans les starting blocks
Pour ce lancement, les partenaires invités par Qualcomm à présenter leurs premiers terminaux étaient Xiaomi et Lenovo. Le premier était le plus engagé des deux. Non seulement le chinois a annoncé utiliser les deux puces, non seulement, mais en plus Adam Zeng, responsable de la division internationale de Xiaomi, a assuré que les 18 Pro et 18 Pro Max (le premier en version classique, le second en version Extreme) seront bien disponibles en Europe – ce qui ne fut pas le cas des versions 17 Pro et 17 Pro Max.
Du côté de Lenovo, la marque sino-américaine a présenté son Signature 27, qui sera le premier terminal de la marque à inaugurer le partenariat audio qui vient tout juste de se nouer avec la marque Bang et Olufsen (B&O).
Mais si une ribambelle d’autres partenaires devrait annoncer leurs terminaux dans les semaines et mois qui viennent, il faudra regarder de près le ratio de marques – notamment chinoises – qui continuent de lancer des fleurons équipés en puces MediaTek. Car la montée en puissance du Taïwanais qui attaque le marché du haut de gamme depuis 2023, celui-ci n’a cessé de grappiller des parts de marché au géant américains.
La question pour Qualcomm est donc de savoir si ses Snapdragon 8 Elite de 6e génération sauront – ou non – faire la différence.

articles.title: Der Jobmarkt für Berufseinsteiger ist um zwei Drittel eingebrochen: Welche Rolle spielt KI dabei?
articles.text:
Stellenangebot für Berufseinsteiger sinkt rasant – außer in zwei Branchen
Wer aktuell in Deutschland nach einem neuen Job sucht, könnte auf Probleme stoßen. Das zeigen derzeit mehrere Analysen und Studien. Zuletzt hatte das Portal Stepstone etwa gezeigt, dass viele Menschen lieber an ihrem aktuellen Job festhalten, statt sich auf die Suche nach etwas Neuem zu begeben. Und das selbst dann, wenn sie unglücklich sind und keine Aufstiegschancen in der aktuellen Position sehen. Jetzt folgt eine weitere Analyse vom Jobportal Indeed, die sich auf Berufseinsteiger fokussiert.
Indeed-Analyse: So schwer haben es Berufseinsteiger
Für die Analyse hat Indeed zunächst Stellenausschreibungen in Deutschland seit 2019 ausgewertet. Um die Stellen für Berufseinsteiger herauszufiltern, wurden Begriffe wie „Junior“, „Berufseinstieg“, „Trainee“, „Absolvent“ und „Young Professional“ als Kriterium herangezogen. Ausbildungsstellen wurden hingegen über Begriffe wie „Ausbildung“, „Lehrstelle“, „Azubi“ oder „Duales Studium“ definiert.
Laut Indeed zeigt sich, dass die Zahl der Berufseinstiegsjobs von 2019 bis 2022 noch angestiegen ist. Im Juli 2022 zeigte sich dann der Höchststand mit einem Plus von 75 Prozent im Vergleich zu 2019. Seither geht es allerdings wieder mit den Jobs für junge Menschen bergab. Die Stellenangebote für Einsteiger sind laut Indeed in der Zwischenzeit um mehr als zwei Drittel gefallen. In derselben Zeit verlor zwar auch der Gesamtmarkt an der Zahl der Stellenanzeigen, allerdings nur um ein Drittel.
Ausbildungen helfen am Jobmarkt aus
Von diesem Rückgang sind laut Indeed fast alle Bereiche betroffen. In 26 von 28 untersuchten Berufsgruppen konnte ein sinkendes Jobangebot verzeichnet werden. 23 davon sind ebenfalls stärker als der Gesamtmarkt betroffen. Dazu gehören primär Bürojobs in den Bereichen Marketing, IT und Projektmanagement. Nur in den Bereichen Pflege, Medizin und Pharmazie sowie Lebensmittel, Gastronomie und Hotellerie wurden mehr Jobs für Einsteiger verzeichnet, wobei diese auch größtenteils über Ausbildungen erfolgen.
Wie Indeed betont, zeichnet sich bei Ausbildung auch ein gänzlich anderes Bild. Im Vergleich zu 2019 wurden von August 2025 bis Juli 2026 etwa 50 Prozent mehr Ausbildungsplätze ausgeschrieben. Hier geht im Vergleich zum Höchststand das Niveau zwar auch zurück, aber deutlich langsamer als bei Einstiegsjobs. In 20 von 23 Gruppen hat sich das Angebot besser entwickelt als in den Pendants der Einstiegsjobs.
Wie KI den Jobmarkt beeinflusst
Virginia Sondergeld, Ökonomin und Arbeitsmarktexpertin bei Indeed, sagte zu den Ergebnissen: „Wer heute ins Berufsleben startet, hat nur noch gut halb so viele Stellen zur Auswahl wie vor wenigen Jahren. Damit steigt für junge Menschen das Risiko, ihre Karriere mit einer Phase der Beschäftigungslosigkeit zu beginnen. Aus Studien wissen wir, dass dies langfristige Narben in ihren Erwerbsbiografien hinterlassen kann, etwa in Form niedrigerer Gehälter, die sich später nur schwer aufholen lassen. Es droht ein Jahrgang, der mit einem Startnachteil ins Erwerbsleben geht.“
Als Ursache sieht die Expertin nur teilweise KI. Die Tools können „Routineaufgaben übernehmen, die traditionell von Berufseinsteigern erledigt wurden“. Die Datenlage gibt aber keinen Anlass für einen belegbaren „KI-Effekt“, da der Rückgang schon vor der Veröffentlichung von ChatGPT zu verzeichnen war. Als größeren Treiber sieht Sondergeld die „schwache Konjunktur, weil Unternehmen in unsicheren Zeiten zuerst dort sparen, wo sie in Nachwuchs investieren müssten. Die wirksamste Hilfe für diese Generation ist deshalb eine Wirtschaft, die wieder wächst.“
Junge Menschen sollten deshalb jetzt genau überlegen, ob sie nach einem Einstiegsjob oder einer Ausbildung suchen, wie Sondergeld betont: „Eine Ausbildung findet im Betrieb statt, der seinen Nachwuchs für den eigenen Bedarf qualifizieren kann und häufig übernimmt. Dass Unternehmen auch in schwachen Jahren an der Ausbildung festhalten und somit jungen Menschen Perspektiven bieten können, trägt dazu bei, dass Deutschland eine der niedrigsten Jugendarbeitslosenquoten in Europa hat. Dieser Vorteil bleibt aber nur erhalten, wenn die Ausbildungsinhalte mit der KI-Transformation Schritt halten und Auszubildende nicht Aufgaben lernen, die in wenigen Jahren eine Maschine erledigt.“

articles.title: Apple could take on Whoop with a new fitness tracker, report says | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Apple is in the process of developing a new screen-less fitness tracker that would put it into competition with Whoop — the fitness tech firm whose valuation recently crested $10 billion.
Bloomberg reports that the iPhone maker is currently engaged in a “technology investigation” — which, just as it sounds, is an exploratory effort to decide whether it will fully develop a product and release it. A number of prototypes have been developed around the item, the outlet notes.
The device — which is described as “a thin fabric band with a sensor-equipped computing module” — would not be released until at least 2028, Bloomberg said.
It’s worth noting that Apple already sells a fitness tracker in the form of its Apple Watch (the wearable records workouts, heart rate, sleep, and other categories). However, the new form factor sounds relatively similar to Whoop, which sells simple fitness bands that the company says can track a variety of health metrics.
TechCrunch reached out to Apple for more information.
The report arrives at a time when Apple is in a period of transition. Tim Cook stepped down from his position as CEO in August to now act as executive chairman, as new CEO John Ternus took the wheel. The company has also faced headwinds due to rising costs from a memory shortage. Despite this, it has promised a slate of new devices, including a new foldable phone, new tablets, and a new MacBook Pro. Meanwhile, it’s engaged in litigation against OpenAI, which it has accused of trade theft, as the battle to build the best hardware for the AI age continues.

articles.title: QNAP Launches Compact TS-432XeU Short-Depth 10 GbE/2.5 GbE Quad-Core ARM NAS
articles.text:
Tuesday, September 22nd 2026
	
									
	
	
	
QNAP Launches Compact TS-432XeU Short-Depth 10 GbE/2.5 GbE Quad-Core ARM NAS
QNAP Systems, Inc., a leading computing, networking and storage solution innovator, today launched the new short-depth rackmount NAS TS-432XeU. Featuring high-speed 10GbE/2.5GbE connectivity, a quad-core ARM processor, flexible expansion and backup options, and support for Docker container applications, the TS-432XeU enables small and medium-sized businesses to quickly build a reliable, high-performance, and easy-to-manage storage and collaboration environment—while minimizing deployment costs.
Sean Teng, Product Manager at QNAP"Designed with both performance and space efficiency in mind, the TS-432XeU combines 10GbE/2.5GbE networking and four USB 3.2 Gen 1 ports to support external backup, fast data ingestion, and flexible capacity expansion. Whether handling daily backups or supporting multi-user collaboration, the TS-432XeU delivers efficient performance while giving SMBs greater operational flexibility and lower long-term storage costs."
TS-432XeU Key Features
TS-432XeU: 1U short-depth rackmount NAS; powered by an AnnapurnaLabs AL324 quad-core 1.7 GHz processor; 4 GB non-ECC RAM (ECC supported, expandable up to 16 GB); 4 × 3.5-inch / 2.5-inch SATA 6 Gbps HDD/SSD bays; 2 × 2.5GbE RJ45 ports, 1 × 10GbE SFP+ port; 4 × USB 3.2 Gen 1 (5 Gbps) ports
		
		Source:
				QNAP			
	
	
	
		
	
		
Sean Teng, Product Manager at QNAP"Designed with both performance and space efficiency in mind, the TS-432XeU combines 10GbE/2.5GbE networking and four USB 3.2 Gen 1 ports to support external backup, fast data ingestion, and flexible capacity expansion. Whether handling daily backups or supporting multi-user collaboration, the TS-432XeU delivers efficient performance while giving SMBs greater operational flexibility and lower long-term storage costs."
- Maximized space efficiency: With a short-depth 1U chassis measuring just 292.1 mm (12 inches) deep, the TS-432XeU fits easily into small racks or wall-mounted network cabinets—making it ideal for offices, factories, multimedia AV rooms, vehicle-based installations, or compact server rooms where space is limited.
- Quad-core ARM processor: Powered by the AnnapurnaLabs 64-bit quad-core 1.7 GHz processor, the TS-432XeU delivers stable performance with low power consumption, making it well suited for everyday business storage, backups, containerized services, and simultaneous multi-user access.
- Flexible capacity expansion: Storage capacity can be expanded by connecting QNAP short-depth JBOD enclosures or higher-capacity expansion units such as the 12-bay TL-R1200C-RP, allowing businesses to scale storage economically for backups, archiving, or long-term data retention.
- High-speed network connectivity: Features one 10GbE SFP+ port and two 2.5GbE RJ45 ports, the TS-432XeU supports Port Trunking and SMB Multichannel to increase available bandwidth—ideal for high-speed data transfers, large file access, and backup and recovery tasks.
- Efficient external connectivity and data ingestion: Four USB 3.2 Gen 1 (5 Gbps) ports allow fast data import from multiple USB storage devices or external backups, and also support QNAP USB expansion devices for greater storage flexibility.

articles.title: Motorola unveils Signature 27 first with Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme
articles.text:
Today at the Snapdragon Summit, which Qualcomm flew me out to, Motorola unveiled the first handset with the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 mobile platform: the Signature 27. Firstly, we’re waiting to hear if the Signature 27 is coming to Canada, but the Motorola press release says it’s a North American release, so I wouldn’t be shocked if it shows up in the North.
Last year’s Motorola Signature wasn’t available in Canada, but we’ll keep our hopes up. Considering the jump from 2025’s Snapdragon 8 Gen 5 to the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, this handset is definitely getting a bump in performance compared to its predecessor. Motorola has also announced that it’s partnered with Bang & Olufsen to power the device’s sound.
The Signature 27 features a Motorola ArcticMesh cooling system, which uses a new diamond-infused thermal gel, liquid metal, copper mesh and a redesigned 3D vapour chamber to help with heating during sustained use.
Additionally, you’ll get a 50MP Sony Lytia 910 primary shooter and a 200MP periscope telephoto lens. And the device has Motorola’s Video Enhancement Engine, which uses AI to create a real-time intelligence layer that adjusts colour tones by analyzing the scene during and even before recording.
Of course, since it’s Motorola, the company has launched the device in two Pantone finishes: Coal Smoke, with a woven texture for better grip strength and durability. And Pantone Capulet Green with a brushed look that looks incredibly nice.
We’re waiting to learn a lot more about the Signature 27, including pricing and availability.

articles.title: Samsung vuelve a retrasar One UI 9 para el Galaxy S26 y ya no da fecha exacta
articles.text:
Si tienes un Galaxy S26, seguramente llevas semanas esperando con ansias la actualización a One UI 9. Aunque Samsung ya liberó la versión estable, su despliegue en el resto del mundo se ha retrasado de forma constante en los últimos días. La mala noticia es que Samsung podría haber movido la fecha una vez más, aunque esta vez se desconoce hasta cuándo estará disponible.
Samsung lanzó la versión estable de One UI 9.0, basada en Android 17, para los Galaxy S26 el 16 de septiembre de 2026. El problema es que eso ocurrió solo en Corea del Sur y la surcoreana no dio detalles sobre cuándo llegaría al resto del mundo. La compañía solo confirmó que los usuarios de Tailandia serían los siguientes en recibirla, con fecha tentativa del 21 de septiembre.
El día esperado llegó y One UI 9 no se liberó en el país asiático, como se tenía contemplado. Poco después, Samsung movió el calendario una semana, eligiendo el 28 de septiembre como nueva fecha para desplegar su sistema operativo. Lo malo es que ahora ni esa fecha parece ser la adecuada, ya que Samsung actualizó los materiales de prensa eliminando la parte donde se mencionaba este despliegue.
Una publicación en la web de Samsung Tailandia solo habla de "septiembre" como fecha tentativa para el lanzamiento de One UI 9, pero sin un día exacto. Aunque muchos ya comenzaron a barajar un nuevo retraso, lo cierto es que el fabricante sigue prometiendo que llegará este mes. Si Samsung mantiene su palabra, el peor escenario posible sería el 30 de septiembre de 2026, todo esto suponiendo que no haya un tercer cambio de planes en el camino.
¿Qué ofrece One UI 9 para el Galaxy S26?
La actualización One UI 9 ofrecerá mejoras, nuevas funciones y varios ajustes a los dueños de un Samsung. Entre las novedades se incluye My FanCam, una función de la cámara que sigue automáticamente a una persona dentro del encuadre y ajusta la toma según su movimiento. Esta característica está pensada para grabar recitales o para usarla en eventos deportivos, sin necesidad de editar después.
Por otro lado, Now Brief recibe tarjetas generativas y editables que nos permitirán personalizar la información que aparece en nuestro resumen diario. En el caso de Now Nudge, este sistema ofrecerá sugerencias contextuales en tiempo real para mejorar la productividad. One UI 9 también incluye Creative Studio, que propone ideas visuales acordes con las fechas señaladas como cumpleaños o festividades.
En seguridad, Samsung debuta Security Brief, una función que centraliza las alertas sobre malware y permisos sospechosos en el móvil. Esta se complementa con las alertas mejoradas de privacidad, que se apoyan en inteligencia artificial para detectar accesos innecesarios en segundo plano. Por último, la actualización también amplía la cobertura contra las estafas telefónicas, de modo que no tendrás que preocuparte cuando recibas llamadas de números que desconoces.
One UI 9 ya está disponible en los Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra, Z Fold8 y Z Flip8. Posteriormente, Samsung ofrecerá la actualización para quienes tengan un Galaxy S26, S25 y Z7, aunque existe la posibilidad de que se libere a más modelos, incluido el Galaxy S23 FE, antes de que finalice el año.

articles.title: ChatGPT débarque dans Microsoft Word, et vous n’avez même pas besoin de payer
articles.text:
OpenAI pousse un peu plus loin l’intégration de ChatGPT aux outils bureautiques de Microsoft. Dans Word, l’assistant travaille désormais directement à partir du document ouvert, même si plusieurs fonctions du chatbot manquent encore à l’appel.
Près de deux ans après son arrivée sur Windows, ChatGPT empiète un peu plus sur les terres de Copilot et débarque officiellement dans Microsoft Word. OpenAI vient en effet d’étendre au traitement de texte son complément déjà proposé dans Excel et PowerPoint, désormais accessible à tous les comptes, y compris gratuits. L’assistant peut ainsi s’appuyer sur le document ouvert pour le résumer, le corriger ou retravailler un passage, sans multiplier les allers-retours entre applications.
Des fonctions bien intégrées, mais encore quelques absents
Pour en profiter, il faudra d’abord récupérer le complément depuis le Microsoft Marketplace, directement dans Word via Accueil > Compléments, tout à droite du ruban. Une fois le module installé et connecté au compte OpenAI, ChatGPT s’ouvre dans un volet latéral, à côté du document en cours.
Il peut alors résumer l’ensemble du texte, corriger ou reformuler une sélection, transformer quelques consignes en brouillon, mais également reprendre les titres, la structure ou la mise en forme du document.
Cette intégration ne reprend toutefois pas tout ce que ChatGPT connaît déjà de vous. Les échanges lancés dans Word n’apparaissent pas dans l’historique du chatbot, tandis que les informations enregistrées en mémoire et les compétences sauvegardées sur le compte ne sont pas accessibles depuis le complément. L’usage du module est par ailleurs décompté du quota associé à l’offre ChatGPT souscrite et peut, selon la formule, puiser dans une enveloppe partagée avec Codex et d’autres fonctions premium.
Même distinction pour les plugins, qui ne sont pas utilisables depuis Word pour le moment. Les services reliés au compte ChatGPT, comme Outlook, SharePoint, Google Workspace ou Dropbox, peuvent en revanche fournir au complément les informations dont il a besoin.

articles.title: Google's robotics unit Intrinsic open-sources its foundational infrastructure for intelligent robots - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Google’s robotics unit Intrinsic open-sources its foundational infrastructure for intelligent robots
Intrinsic, the intelligent robotics software company owned by Google LLC’s parent Alphabet Inc., said today that it’s open-sourcing the core components of its industrial robotics platform.
Announced at ROSCon 2026 in Toronto today, the new offering is called Intrinsic Core, and its release under a permissive Apache 2.0 license is all about democratizing access to intelligent robotics, the company said. Founded in 2021, Intrinsic was incorporated into Google’s operations in February to accelerate the development of physical AI to push the envelope of artificial intelligence beyond digital applications and into real-world industrial environments.
Physical AI describes AI systems that use sensors, actuators, and control systems to perceive, reason, act and learn in real-world environments. It differs from pure software because it bridges the gap between bits and atoms – allowing autonomous machines such as robots, self-driving cars, drones and smart infrastructure to take action.
Though physical AI is interesting, its progress has long been stalled by the complexity of developing the underlying software and training the AI models that sit at the heart of intelligent robots. Google and Intrinsic both believe that progress can be accelerated with the availability of a reusable, foundational software layer that provides the basic infrastructure for physical AI, so that developers don’t have to rebuild everything from scratch for each new robot they create.
This is where Intrinsic Core should come in handy. It’s a preconfigured, Robot Operating System-compatible software environment designed to run on local hardware. It provides a number of reusable building blocks that developers can integrate with their physical robotics systems, providing them with the capabilities they need to operate in industrial environments.
These building blocks include Intrinsic Control, which is a hardware-agnostic real-time control framework capable of dynamically adapting a robot’s trajectory mid-movement, based on the feedback provided by its sensors. This will make it easier for developers to use various kinds of hardware, such as arms and grippers, without rewriting the underlying software and drivers for them each time, Intrinsic said.
Other components include Pose Estimation, a capability based on Nvidia Corp.’s FoundationPose that enables robots to dynamically detect and handle parts, removing the need for rigid, expensive physical fixtures. There’s also a motion planning capability that automates collision-avoidance path generation, eliminating the need for developers to program robots manually, joint by joint in a position-controlled way. And there’s a grasp planning function that allows various types of robotic grippers to automatically and dynamically adapt to the location and orientation of the objects they’re trying to grasp.
Intrinsic Core also provides simulation and calibration services that make it possible to simulate, visualize and troubleshoot robotics and calibrate their vision systems through a single interface. Finally, there are Intrinsic-ROS drivers, which make it easier for developers to integrate sensors with third-party grippers, 3D cameras and other hardware components.
To showcase how Intrinsic Core can aid robotics developers, the company has also released the Open Machine Tending Solution, which is a kind of open reference design for AI-powered CNC machine tending tasks. It supports modular customization for different hardware setups from major robotics manufacturers, including Universal Robots A/S and FANUC Corp.
Intrinsic said the Open Machine Tending Solution is designed to help accelerate automation in the machine building industry. The company said the U.S. and Europe are home to tens of thousands of shops that fabricate intricate parts for machines in a wide range of industries, yet only 8% of those shops use any form of automation at all due to the high costs and technical barriers of adoption. By providing a customizable starting point, Intrinsic believes, its reference design will pave the way for much smaller fabricators to automate lower-value tasks and accelerate automation.
More broadly, Intrinsic said it hopes to foster the growth of a much broader robotics developer ecosystem based on shared, open-source tools and accelerate the adoption of physical AI in various industries.

articles.title: Claude Opus 5.5 wants to finish your coding tasks, not just start them
articles.text:
Claude Opus 5.5 wants to finish your coding tasks, not just start them
Anthropic wants developers to use Claude and its family of tools to handle complete coding tasks. The company introduced Claude Opus 5.5 on Tuesday to span more of the software application development lifecycle: from design specification creation through debugging to code generation and testing.
As the first release in a new family of Claude 5.5 models, Anthropic says that Claude Opus 5.5 performs at the level of Claude Fable 5.1 on “most work” tasks and costs around 40% less to run than Opus 5.
GitHub chief product officer Mario Rodriguez is quoted in Anthropic’s launch announcement on exactly where software engineers sit today with frontier models for code automation. He said that developers want agents.
“In our testing [of Claude Opus 5.5] across GitHub Copilot CLI and VS Code, Claude Opus 5.5 used among the fewest tokens and steps we measured. In VS Code, it solved more terminal tasks than Opus 5 in less than half the steps. More than making individual tasks more efficient, it’s making developers’ bigger projects more achievable,” says Rodriguez.
Where does Claude Opus 5.5 get its power from?
Anthropic explains that the Claude 5.5 family’s expanded full-lifecycle capabilities were developed under an established set of practices.
These practice elements include extensive alignment testing (model evaluation processes put in place to make sure actions and outputs closely match human values and intended goals), pre-release evaluation by outside organizations, and safeguards for high-risk areas such as cybersecurity and biology.
The organization says that on its most comprehensive alignment test, Opus 5.5 is the strongest-performing model tested to date, with particular improvements in several behaviors that contributed to recent cybersecurity incidents (e.g., biased reasoning, attempting to escape a sandbox, and others).
Independent SRE & AI reliability architect Akash Thakur tells The New Stack that Anthropic’s work getting its model to complete whole coding tasks is impressive, but “getting it to know when it hasn’t” is the harder problem developers need to think about.
“Models working at the level of Claude Opus 5.5 are genuinely good at breaking a project into small, finishable pieces — and that’s the real unlock, because momentum on software comes from finishing things, not starting them,” Thakur says. “…But ‘completed’ and ‘correct’ aren’t the same thing. The task that looks done and completed is exactly the one that often costs the team later, so the win isn’t removing the human — it’s moving them from writing the code to verifying it.”
“Models working at the level of Claude Opus 5.5 are genuinely good at breaking a project into small, finishable pieces …but ‘completed’ and ‘correct’ aren’t the same thing.”
Suggesting that we are now witnessing a “higher bar for more capable models”, Anthropic said that models that could fully automate AI research itself should meet a higher safety standard. The company noted that as AI becomes more capable, public policy should play a larger role in making sure these systems are safe. Its recent work with Accenture is offered as an example of how Anthropic is building the infrastructure to support this.
Sprawling jobs: codebase-wide migrations & audits
Getting more specific, Anthropic has claimed Opus 5.5 is “particularly good” at long, sprawling jobs like codebase-wide migrations and audits. An early tester said it audited and fixed a 200,000-line codebase in under three hours, while Opus 5 took over 20 hours and used 2.5x as many tokens.
“In an internal test, we asked Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 to translate HAProxy, widely used software that balances web traffic loads across servers, from C into Rust. Both rewrites passed nearly all of HAProxy’s own regression tests, but Opus 5.5 finished in 9.5 hours compared to 12 for Fable 5.1, and cost 51% less,” said Anthropic in a press statement.
Field CTO for the EMEA region at Coder, Eric Paulsen, tells The New Stack that he is happy to hear Claude Opus 5.5 is becoming more holistically capable, but he’s “not surprised” because AI is “eating the software delivery chain end to end” today.
“Despite the efficiencies showcased in Opus 5.5, the moment an agent can reliably finish real work, the question stops being whether the model is good enough and becomes where you’re letting it run,” Paulsen says.
“Kicking off a Claude Code session on a laptop that can be compromised, stolen, or simply run out of compute is not an engineering environment; capable agents need dedicated, governed infrastructure with the same guardrails, secrets handling, and observability a developer would demand of any other production workload. As we’ve seen here with Anthropic’s own work, firms need to underline testing and safeguard procedures for launches of this kind,” he added.
Anthropic assures users that external testing has been conducted and that the model was tested before release by Frontier Design and METR. When established safeguards for Opus 5.5 intervene, requests “fall back to another model transparently,” meaning developers may not see which model actually handled a given call.
In cybersecurity, users can identify and fix bugs in their code, but most cybersecurity tasks will be re-routed to Opus 4.8. Requests flagged by biology and frontier LLM development classifiers will be re-routed to Opus 5. Vetted organizations can apply to Anthropic’s Life Sciences Verification Program to use Opus 5.5 for biology research, and the company says it will expand its Cyber Verification Program in the coming weeks.
The developer’s terminal prompt has fundamentally changed
HasData co-founder, Sergey Ermakovich, tells The New Stack that his work as a web scraping specialist for data pipelines and AI means he sees zen-like, one-brick-at-a-time logic in what Anthropic has done.
“The biggest change — and it’s a trend that will have driven Anthropic’s design and development aspirations for Claude Opus 5.5 — is that the terminal is no longer just a place where a developer pastes generated code,” Ermakovich says. “The terminal now becomes part of the model’s workspace.”
Because a model can run commands, inspect failures, modify files, and verify the result, Ermakovich suggests it can “close the loop” instead of handing unfinished work back to an engineer. “That makes small complete tasks much more valuable. Fix one failing test, update one dependency, migrate one endpoint, verify it, then move to the next task,” he adds.
“The terminal is no longer just a place where a developer pastes generated code — the terminal now becomes part of the model’s workspace.”
Commenting on the development of this model as part of Anthropic’s approved corporate messaging, John Ruelas, staff software engineer at Ramp, said that verbose, hard-to-follow output has been his “biggest frustration” with frontier models, but “Claude Opus 5.5 fixes it” for him.
He noted that it writes like a good colleague and follows his company’s writing rules. A design spec came out usable with very minimal edits, and when it rewrote one of his prompts, he preferred its version to his own. When it optimized the team’s test suite, he could follow its reasoning easily and “shipped the change with confidence.”
We’re so done with the autocomplete era
Vice president of AI strategy at Abbyy, Maxime Vermeir, tells The New Stack that the more lifecycle-wide Claude Opus 5.5 features on offer show that “we’re done with the autocomplete era” for basic code automation tools.
“Anthropic’s elevation here reflects the fact that it used to be thought of as marvelous if AI could complete a developer’s next line of code, but today the expectation is that you hand it a whole Jira ticket and that it gets done,” Vermeir says. “But despite the power on show with Claude Opus 5.5, the question remains as to how much these newer models will actually understand what ‘done’ means, as often it seems they have a desire to keep burning tokens by offering you yet another thing it didn’t quite do right.”
Opus 5.5 also “communicates more naturally” than prior models, with early testers finding its writing clearer and easier to follow, making it a better work partner over long sessions.
Costed out lower than Opus 5, Opus 5.5 is priced at $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens (20% less than Opus 5), and Anthropic has cut cache read prices by 60% for token-billed usage. Opus 5.5 also needs fewer tokens for higher-quality work and generates output more than 30% faster than Opus 5.

articles.title: Sweden fines Miljödata $183,000 over breach affecting 2.2 million
articles.text:
Sweden’s data privacy regulator, IMY, has imposed a $183,000 (SEK 1.8 million) fine on IT systems provider Miljödata for inadequate security measures leading to a breach in August 2025 affecting 2.2 million people.
Miljödata is a Swedish software company that develops and provides work environment and HR management systems used by 80% of Sweden’s municipal systems.
Last year, on August 25, the company suffered a cyberattack that disrupted IT services in over 200 regions and compromised residents' sensitive data.
The threat actor demanded a ransom of 1.5 Bitcoin (valued at $168,000 at the time) to prevent leaking the stolen information, but published it on the dark web under the name “Datacarry.”
The information included personal identity numbers, contact information, sickness absence, rehabilitation, and even school incidents involving underage individuals.
IMY launched an investigation in November 2025 to determine whether any security shortcomings violated the company’s obligations under the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).
The agency has now confirmed that the company failed to adequately check newly installed software and lacked automated, real-time monitoring mechanisms to detect intrusions and suspicious activity.
“IMY’s investigation shows that the company did not maintain a sufficiently high level of technical and organizational security, considering the types of personal data it processed,” reads the announcement.
“The company did not perform sufficient checks when installing new software and did not have automated real-time monitoring of its systems to detect intrusions and suspicious activity.”
The negligence constitutes a violation of Article 32(1) of the GDPR, for which the agency imposed a penalty of $183,000.
Threat actors sometimes use the prospect of regulatory penalties to pressure victims into paying, and may set demands below what they believe an incident would ultimately cost, to incentivize victims to pay the ransom.
IMY noted that it has also launched investigations into two municipalities and one region in connection with the attack on Miljödata, which are ongoing, so additional penalties may be imposed in the future.
