articles.title: Renault 5 E-Tech : une autonomie à l’épreuve de la montagne, 409 km engloutis comme si c’était un trajet banal
articles.text:
Renault 5 E-Tech : une autonomie à l’épreuve de la montagne, 409 km engloutis comme si c’était un trajet banal
Sur les routes escarpées des Carpates, la Renault 5 E-Tech a déjoué tous les pronostics en affichant une consommation record sans la moindre recharge. Elle s’est même approchée de l’autonomie WLTP annoncée par le constructeur français.
La citadine électrique n’est pas faite que pour rouler en ville, la Renault 5 E-Tech vient d’ailleurs de le démontrer haut la main. Engagée dans le périple roumain Eurocharge 2026 du média Autocritica, ce modèle tricolore a relié Pitești à Alba Iulia en franchissant les Carpates, et ce, sans pause pour recharger. De quoi confirmer qu’une batterie modeste peut parfaitement encaisser les longs trajets, et donc rassurer les plus sceptiques sur les capacités de la voiture électrique face aux modèles thermiques.
La R5 E-Tech maîtrise ses basiques avec une autonomie à un cheveu du cycle WLTP
Sur un parcours exigeant de 309 kilomètres reliant Pitești à Alba Iulia, la déclinaison Roland Garros de 148 chevaux de la Renault 5 E-Tech s’est frottée à la célèbre Transalpina, un col spectaculaire culminant à 2 145 mètres d’altitude.
Loin d’un test d’éco-conduite aseptisé, l’essai s’est déroulé en conditions réelles, avec deux personnes à bord et des bagages. Tudor Rus, journaliste pour le média roumain Autocritica, résume son enthousiasme : “Petite, vive et amusante par endroits, surtout sur les lacets de la Transalpina. Je ne la cantonnerais pas au cliché de la citadine”.
Le tracé alternait portions à 90 km/h, longues ascensions montagnardes, phases de descente très régénératrices et près de 18 % d’autoroute avalés à 130 km/h. À l’arrivée, le verdict énergétique a dissipé toutes les appréhensions avec une consommation moyenne de seulement 12,7 kWh aux 100 km. La Renault 5 E-Tech a ainsi rallié l’étape d’une seule traite, sans ravitaillement et sans finir à bout de souffle. “Nous sommes arrivés à l’hôtel sans encombre, avec 16 % de batterie et une autonomie restante de 95 kilomètres affichée au compteur”, précise le journaliste.
Rapportée aux 52 kWh de sa batterie, cela donne une autonomie théorique de 409 kilomètres, tutoyant les 410 kilomètres de l’homologation WLTP mixte officielle pour le modèle sorti avant la mise à jour de septembre 2026.
Une performance qui vient balayer d’un revers de main la fameuse angoisse de la panne qui nourrit encore le scepticisme vis-à-vis de l’autonomie dite limitée des voitures électriques. Renault prouve ici qu’une conception sobre et légère surpasse la course aux grosses batteries, permettant à une simple citadine d’avaler les kilomètres et le relief en toute sérénité.

articles.title: OpenAI releases GPT-6 Sol and Luna — and cuts token prices in half
articles.text:
OpenAI releases GPT-6 Sol and Luna — and cuts token prices in half
OpenAI on Tuesday released GPT-6 Sol and Luna, which will complement the flagship GPT-6 Astra model in OpenAI’s lineup. As of now, there is no GPT-6 Terra.
The new GPT-6 pricing
The headline news here is that OpenAI cut the price per million input/output tokens by half or more, compared to the previous version. GPT-6 Sol will cost $2/$10 per million input/output tokens (vs. $4/$20 for GPT-5.6 Sol), and GPT-6 Luna will come in at $0.10/$0.50 (vs. $0.20/$1.20).
The GPT-5.6 pricing was always meant to be promotional, but for the new GPT-6 models, this is the default price, an OpenAI spokesperson tells The New Stack.
“Improvements in caching and inference let us serve these models at lower cost, and we’re passing those savings directly on to users and customers,” OpenAI explains in its announcement.
Benchmarks
As you would expect, the new models show clear improvements over the GPT-5.6 predecessors, but for the most part, these are not all that extreme.
On a benchmark like Zapier’s AutomationBench — which checks how well the models work on a set of business workflow tests — GPT-6 Luna improves by 5.4 percentage points over the previous version, for example
On the DeepSWE v1.1 software engineering benchmark, GPT-6 Sol essentially matches Anthropic’s Fable (68.8% at max effort vs. 69.9% for Fable 5 at xhigh effort), but at only 20% of the cost. Luna, at max effort, hits scores similar to Claude Opus 5 and Fable 5 at medium effort, at a significantly lower cost.
And OpenAI focuses on this cost comparison across its announcement—with a special focus on price per task instead of straight-up token pricing.
Anthropic resets the comparison
Since Anthropic released Opus 5.5 earlier on Tuesday, OpenAI’s comparisons are already out of date — such is the way of this AI era. Anthropic, too, reduced its per-token pricing for Opus 5.5 to $4/$20, down from $5/$25, but that still leaves Anthropic’s model twice as expensive as the comparable GPT-6 Sol.
In its announcement, when comparing GPT-6 Sol to Opus 5, OpenAI was able to claim significant cost savings when compared to Anthropic’s model — and for the most part that still holds, but Anthropic says Opus 5.5 also uses fewer tokens per task, which, according to the company, works out to 40% lower costs than Opus 5 on typical workloads.
It’s worth noting that no one has run Sol and Opus 5.5 head-to-head yet. Sol likely stays cheaper per task on OpenAI’s AutomationBench numbers, but Opus 5.5 posts higher scores than GPT-5.6 Sol on shared benchmarks in Anthropic’s testing.
Since it’s almost impossible to know how many tokens an agent will use to finish a task, though, these pricing changes still don’t make it any easier for a user to budget.
Prompt caching
For developers building agents, the caching changes may matter more than token prices. OpenAI says it improved prompt caching for GPT-6 to deliver higher cache hit rates by default, with discounts of up to 90% on cached input tokens.
One positive change, too, is that developers can now change the reasoning effort and tool availability without invalidating the cache. With explicit breakpoints, developers can choose where a cached prefix ends, and a new dashboard and diagnostics tool show what’s getting cached and what isn’t.
GitHub says these improvements cut the share of prompt tokens that require fresh processing by more than half over the past several months, across billions of requests to OpenAI models.
Anthropic made a similar move with Opus 5.5, which cuts cache read prices by 60% for token-billed usage, on top of the 20% per-token cut.
Style changes
Models aren’t just about benchmarks, though. With GPT-6 Sol, OpenAI made its models answer more directly, rather than in the previous — already reined-in — more conversational style. “Expect to see more clarity, less jargon, fewer odd turns of phrase, fewer low-value details, and slightly shorter answers overall without losing substance,” OpenAI says.
Alignment
Given the HuggingFace incident, it’s no surprise OpenAI is emphasizing its alignment work for GPT-6 Sol and Luna, too.
OpenAI says both models improve on their GPT-5.6 counterparts across its alignment evaluations, including fewer misleading claims about their own coding work. On an internal coding deception test, GPT-6 Sol’s rate fell to 1.3% from 10.4%.
When given a deliberately broken search tool — and graded on whether it disclosed the problem instead of guessing — Sol failed to disclose the problem 4.9% of the time, down from 77.5%.
What is a bit more concerning, though, is that when researchers asked the model to respect an explicit warning like an “access denied” message, GPT-6 Sol still tried to work around those restrictions in 64.4% of runs, down only slightly from 68.2% for its predecessor. Luna improved more, to 42.4% from 76.5%.
OpenAI says these tests cover mostly low-stakes situations and run without full system-level safeguards used in its products.
On a simulated message board seeded with unauthorized instructions, including requests to disclose private information, Sol took the specified action in 11.3% of runs where it found the board, down from 51.9%. Luna and Astra took none, though OpenAI notes Luna also found the board less often.
Anthropic, by contrast, says Opus 5.5 is the strongest performer on its most comprehensive alignment test and names METR and Frontier Design as pre-release external testers. Opus 5.5 also ships with safeguards that reroute requests, sending most cybersecurity tasks to Opus 4.8 and anything flagged by Anthropic’s biology or frontier LLM development classifiers to Opus 5.
Availability
GPT-6 Sol and Luna are available in ChatGPT Work and Codex starting Tuesday for Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu users.
Free and Go users get Luna in the desktop app.
Neither model is in Chat yet. OpenAI says it plans to roll them out gradually throughout the day to keep service stable, so they may not appear right away.

articles.title: A driverless Waymo car wandered into a farmers market, and nobody knew how to stop it
articles.text:
Facepalm: Waymo self-driving taxis might crash less often than human drivers, but they're far from perfect, and when they do something wrong, how do people let them know? That was the issue that appeared recently when a Waymo entered a farmers market as stall owners were setting up their stands.
The vehicle entered Denver's South Pearl Street Farmers Market on Sunday, September 20. Assistant market manager Shari Wilkins told 9News (via The Denver Gazette) that it arrived around 8:40 am, 20 minutes before the market was due to open.
Despite barricades and signs, the car made its way into the market, leaving workers trying to stop it and clear its path.
Market manager Nicole Jarman told Denver7 that the barricades were moved aside during setup to allow vendors' vehicles through. The Waymo followed that traffic flow inside.
Jarman said the vehicle was not driving recklessly, and no injuries were reported. But the incident left organizers wondering how to warn a vehicle that has no driver.
Jarman said the city had contacted her and would approach Waymo through Denver's Department of Transportation and Infrastructure to establish what workers should do if it happened again. Waymo said would learn from the incident as it continued improving safety.
A company spokesperson said the vehicle had already been navigating toward a destination on South Pearl Street when setup began. Waymo maintained that its system recognized the situation and maneuvered out of the market.
In July, it was reported that an independent Insurance Institute for Highway Safety analysis found Waymo vehicles had a 68% lower rate of police-reportable crashes than human drivers.
Across roughly 50 million autonomous miles, the rates were 1.28 crashes per million miles for Waymo and 4.06 for humans. Researchers adjusted for differences in reporting minor collisions, although operating conditions and comparisons with average drivers make the headline figures better than they sound.
Accountability for self-driving cars is also changing. California's new rules allow police to issue notices of noncompliance to autonomous vehicle manufacturers. The process gives authorities a route to report alleged traffic violations even when nobody is behind the wheel.
Denver's market encounter might not have been a crash, but it highlights another problem with autonomous vehicles. People sharing streets with robotaxis need to know how to get their attention when something goes wrong.
A far more serious incident in 2023 saw a Cruise robotaxi drag a pedestrian, who had been struck by another car, underneath its wheels, prompting a nationwide pause. GM later ended Cruise's robotaxi development. While nobody was hurt in Denver, the encounter again raises questions about how autonomous vehicles handle unexpected situations.

articles.title: 'Among my favorite headphones of the year': I reviewed the Sonos Ace Ultra and their impeccable sound, excellent ANC and a stunning design means they can finally go toe-to-toe with Sony and Bose
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
With a significant improvement in musicality, excellent Dolby Atmos performance, and a more fleshed-out feature set, the Sonos Ace Ultra feel like a landmark achievement for Sonos, which has finally entered the headphone game with confidence. Incremental additions to battery life, ANC, and Sonos ecosystem interactivity only help these stylish cans to stand-out more than the original model, and while the Ace Ultra may still get edged out by a few rivals in terms of sonic detail and travel convenience, they’re still easy to recommend.
Pros
- +Far more musical than the Ace
- +Excellent Dolby Atmos for movies
- +Fantastic feature-suite with enhanced ANC and detailed EQ options
- +Stunning design; responsive controls
Cons
- -Some rivals still offer more detail
- -Case doesn’t mirror the headphones’ premium look and feel
- -Not fully foldable
Why you can trust TechRadar
Sonos Ace Ultra: two-minute review
Sonos is making a real statement of intent with its new wireless headphones, the Sonos Ace Ultra.
The multi-room master has made a whole host of improvements to this upgraded wireless over-ear model, which has arrived two years after the original Ace came to market. The Sonos Ace Ultra have enhanced custom 40mm drivers, a new headphone engine, better battery life, better noise-cancelling, and more detailed EQ to name a few things. So can they finally compete with flagship rivals from the likes of Sony and Bose to become some of the best noise-cancelling headphones we've tested? Here’s what I think after weeks of testing.
Let’s start by addressing the most important area of all: sound quality. We felt that the original Ace fell short of the best headphones around due to one main issue: their middling musicality. But the Ace Ultra have remedied that, and then some.
When listening to the Sonos Ace Ultra beside the original model, the differences were stark. Where the standard Sonos Ace sounded confined, overstretched, and unrefined, the Ace Ultra offered openness, intricate detailing, and a broader, more organized soundstage. What’s more, they provide better balance across the frequency range, with deep yet controlled bass, rich but less overzealous mids, and tight, articulate treble.
While I still consider some similarly priced competitors, like the Sony WH-1000XM6 and Bowers & Wilkins Px7 S3 to supply slightly more premium, detailed sound (for music, that is), the Ace Ultra are really not far behind. Sonos listened to the critics, and proved that it's up to the task of going toe-to-toe with the titans of the headphone world.
We already loved the original Ace for movies, though, finding that they offered immersive Dolby Atmos audio with effective head-tracking to boot. And that’s much the same on the Ace Ultra. They whip up wonderful width, strong command over height effects, and never neglect the fundamentals like clear dialogue and cinematic, pounding bass.
But what’s new on the Ace Ultra? Although music got a seismic upgrade, other alterations feel a bit more incremental — but that’s by no means a bad thing. Two more microphones have been added to the Ultra, bringing the total to ten, and ANC is great here. Wherever I was, my soundings were subdued to great effect, almost creating a bubble of silence. ANC is adaptive this time around and adjusts nicely, and the transparency mode works a treat. Call quality is strong too, as you may expect.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Battery life has also seen a boost, and you’ll now get up to 35 hours with ANC on. Is this anything groundbreaking? No. But it’s slightly above the 30-hour standard for headphones in this price bracket, and I never felt that I had to charge these cans very regularly. The battery is also replaceable, and a rapid charging mode means you can get three hours of playback if you spend three minutes juicing them up.
EQ options have also been expanded beyond the basic two-band equalizer found on the standard Ace headphones. There’s an eight-band option now as well as adaptive EQ, meaning you can genuinely tailor sound to your specific tastes.
We also need to talk about the Wi-Fi capabilities of the Sonos Ace Ultra. No, we’re still not at the point where we can directly stream tunes over a local internet connection, but there are some nifty features at play. First of all, TV Audio Swap is back, enabling you to link the headphones to a compatible Sonos soundbar, and transfer sound seamlessly. This is highly responsive and effective, and while I didn’t find myself using this feature a ton, you can avoid the latency issues you’d get from connecting headphones to your TV over Bluetooth.
The Ace Ultra also add Headphone Linking, though, which means you can also transfer sound from compatible speakers, like the Sonos Play, for instance. This is equally reliable as TV Audio Swap, and is a great option if you’re listening to music at home but want to keep listening without distracting others.
It’s clear to see that the Sonos Ace Ultra don’t look very different from the previous model, but that’s no bad thing. They’re sleek, well-built, and offer a neat combination of comfort and over-ear security. They’re not fully foldable, and the included case could be better quality-wise, but these are fairly minor pain points in the grand scheme of things.
Considering that the Ace Ultra cost the same as the original Ace at the point of launch — and actually less in the UK — they feel like a much more worthwhile investment. They’re by no means cheap, but their enhancements are meaningful and substantial, making these a great pair of headphones whether you have a pre-existing Sonos system or not. As a result, these are a great pair of headphones for music and movie lovers alike that feel worth the outlay — and are easy to recommend if you want a great all-round pair of premium wireless headphones.
Sonos Ace Ultra review: price & release date
- Priced at $449 / £399 / AU$699
- First released September 2026
The Sonos Ace Ultra were released in September 2026, about two years after the original Sonos Ace headphones. The new model is priced at $449 / £399 / AU$699, which is the same as the standard Ace cost at launch in the US and Australia, though they’re actually cheaper in the UK than the original Ace were at the point of release.
Given their price, the Ace Ultra have some extremely hot competition. For example, the Sony WH-1000XM6 are similarly priced, and offer an incredible mix of balanced, dynamic, and impactful sound alongside some of the best noise-cancelling on the market and a giant suite of features. Other competitors include the noise-crushing Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones Gen 2, the spacious sounding Bowers & Wilkins Px7 S3, and the ultra-detailed Sennheiser HDB 630.
Sonos Ace Ultra review: specs
| Drivers | Next-gen 40mm custom | 
| Active noise cancellation | Yes | 
| Battery life | 35 hours (ANC on) | 
| Weight | 0.7lbs / 322g | 
| Connectivity | Bluetooth 6.0, USB-C | 
| Frequency range | 20Hz-20kHz | 
Sonos Ace Ultra review: features
- Excellent ANC with adaptive mode and effective transparency option
- Higher-res audio available as well as Dolby Atmos for spatial sound
- TV Audio Swap and Headphone Linking works very well
The Sonos Ace Ultra boast an excellent suite of features and are a highly personalizable, smart set of headphones.
Let’s kick off with ANC, which has had quite the revamp. Now, you can toggle on an adaptive mode, which adjusts for things like fit, whether you’re wearing glasses, and if you make sudden head movements. But that’s not all.
Sonos has also boosted the number of mics for the Ultra, with ten to the original Ace’s eight. The mics can monitor your surroundings and cut out external noise in real time, and they do this to great effect. Yes, the Ace Ultra supply great ANC, and no matter my environment, I was treated to satisfying, distraction-free listening.
When out on walks, the sounds of cars passing by were totally nullified. When typing away in the office, the clacking of keyboards was fully subdued, and when travelling on public transport, engine sounds and surrounding chatter were put right to the sword. The Aware Mode is also very effective, and makes it incredibly easy to tune into your surroundings, with the new Voice Boost mode able to improve the clarity of voices around you if you toggle it on.
The upgraded microphone system also helps the Ace Ultra to handle phone calls with greater care than ever before. When taking calls when out and about, my speech was perfectly comprehensible, and never sounded obscured by background noise, even when walking in a busy part of my city.
Something else that’s received a boost is battery life. Sonos says that the Ace Ultra are capable of staying alive for 35 hours on a single charge, and my testing found this to be pretty accurate. This is a slight improvement on the original Ace, which could deliver 30 hours of use, which is essentially the standard for headphones in this price category. There’s also a rapid charging option, which gives the Ace Ultra three hours of playback from a three minute charge and a power saving mode if you want to extend the headphones’ life in a pinch.
One of the more welcome additions to the Ace Ultra is their expanded EQ options. Now, you can make use of an eight-band equalizer to customize the sound of the headphones to your specific taste. This is a big improvement on the basic two-band equalizer on the original Ace (for bass and treble levels), though there’s a more basic three-band option on the Ace Ultra if you prefer a less detail-oriented approach.
Let’s stick with sound, because there are a number of great features here that help you get the best out of both music and movies. First of all, you get all the hi-res goodness from the original Ace, with aptX codec support, as well as lossless audio via USB-C — and there’s a USB-C to 3.5mm cable bundled if you want to use them with a laptop, DJ controller, or other source device.
Dolby Atmos also returns on the Ace Ultra, enabling you to enjoy spatial audio on the go. Once again, this works an absolute treat — especially for movies, where head-tracking also helps to further immerse you in on-screen action. I tried using the TV Audio Swap feature, which enabled me to connect the headphones to the Sonos Beam Ultra, and Atmos movies sounded wonderful — more on that in the ‘sound quality’ section.
While the situations in which I’d use TV Audio Swap are admittedly niche, it's a very reliable feature. It harnesses Wi-Fi connectivity, so you don’t have to deal with the latency issues that connecting headphones to your TV over Bluetooth would bring. And you can easily switch between the soundbar, headphones, and other compatible Sonos speakers with a simple press of a button, which is highly convenient.
The Ace Ultra’s new Headphone Engine 2 also enables Headphone Linking, which allows them to directly connect to other components in your Sonos system — including compatible speakers such as the Sonos play — and move audio to and from your speakers and headphones. Like TV Audio Swap, this feels seamless and speedy to activate, and is great if you’re blasting music at home, but don’t want to disturb others if they want some peace and quiet.
On top of all of this, you get the usual good stuff: multi-point pairing, Bluetooth 6.0 connectivity, wear detection, and a relatively intuitive companion app. And when you add all of this together, I think it's fair to say that the Ace Ultra offer an incredibly fleshed-out, and well-refined feature set.
- Features score: 5/5
Sonos Ace Ultra review: sound quality
- Big improvement over original Ace with better soundstaging, detailing, and control
- Deep, immersive bass, clean mids, and tight, expressive treble
- Fantastic Dolby Atmos performance
While we considered the original Sonos Ace to be a good pair of headphones, their somewhat middling musicality ended up holding them back from greatness. But luckily, Sonos has listened to the criticism, implemented next-gen 40mm custom drivers, and remedied a lot of the issues we had with the previous model. The result? A genuinely great-sounding pair of headphones.
I tried comparing the Sonos Ace Ultra against the original model directly, and when I say that the difference is striking, I truly mean it. In essence, the Ace Ultra provide a significantly broader soundstage with far better organization and balance, as well as deeper, more controlled bass, and more articulate, detailed treble. I also found them to offer superior handling of dynamics and enhanced instrument separation, meaning that, for me, Sonos is closer to rivals like Bose and Sony than ever before.
Sonos has been keen to talk up the Ace Ultra’s improved bass, so I started out by listening to a house track, Get It On by Jansons. The Ace Ultra delivered palpable, pumping bass, that was rhythmic and rapid, never sounding lethargic or boomy. This never concealed other sounds across the frequency range, either, with synths in the mid-range sounding well defined and tonally accurate, and high-pitched drums coming through with precision and vigor, helping the track to maintain its high energy.
Treble was especially tighter on the Ace Ultra compared to the original model, and the wider soundstage gave each individual element more room to breathe, and this became a theme across all of my listening tests.
For instance, with the funk track Joía Rara by Brylho, the upgrade the Ultra provided was considerable. On the original Sonos Ace, the soundstage felt confined, with guitars lacking definition in the mix, and as the track built, the horns, bass, vocals, and guitars sounded slightly convoluted, resulting in a messier presentation than I’d expected. But on the Ace Ultra, things were totally different. Guitars in the intro occupied a unique pocket, bass was well-balanced, and finer percussive details were perfectly audible. Vocals were also separated to greater effect, and while they weren’t the most textured or forward, they were more than clear enough.
Are the Sonos Ace Ultra the best-sounding headphones in their price bracket? Well, they’re not far behind the competition, though I do still think a couple of models edge just ahead. For example, I tested them side by side with the Sony WH-1000XM6, and I found that Sony’s cans supplied a slightly more dynamic low-end output and detailing in the mid-range. It was very close between these two, though. Of course, if you want the most expansive soundstage, headphones like the AirPods Max 2 will edge out the Ace Ultra, but they’re slightly more expensive.
Before we move onto design, we have to talk about the Ace Ultra’s handling of spatial audio. They support Dolby Atmos as well as head tracking, really helping you to immerse yourself in your favorite movies and TV shows, and the expansiveness that the headphones supply is seriously impressive.
When using TV Audio Swap with some 4K UHD Blu-ray discs, the Ace Ultra were able to conjure up an excellent sense of width, almost like some of the best Dolby Atmos soundbars can. I started by watching Elio, and the Ace Ultra did an incredible job — voices were clear, and as characters moved across the screen, they were tracked with precision, and if I tilted my head, sound shifted dynamically as if I was speaking with characters directly. As Elio returned to earth, deep, pounding bass hit with immense power too, but didn’t sound muddy or overbearing.
With Godzilla Minus One, the sense of a plane flying overhead in the opening scene was captured far more effectively than expected. It was genuinely convincing, as if the sound was truly coming from above. Dialogue was clear again, and Godzilla’s almighty screech was both tonally accurate and controlled, rather than tinny. More generally, the movie’s action scenes had tremendous width, creating a genuinely immersive experience.
- Sound quality score: 4.5/5
Sonos Ace Ultra review: design
- Beautiful design, and very well made
- Comfortable yet secure fit
- Not fully foldable, but case included for added security
The Ace Ultra look an awful lot like the original Ace, but as someone who loved the way those headphones looked, that’s a big plus. The ear cups are relatively flat and understated, the rounded look is sleek and sexy, and the metallic details only add to the sense of premium. The button controls have shifted about slightly, but they’re incredibly easy to reach, and are all very responsive.
I tried the Soft White version which is stylish and modern, but the Ace Ultra are also available in Black, Agave, and Sand. All of these colorways are minimalistic and suit the luxurious vibe of the headphones to perfection.
In terms of fit, the Ace Ultra strike a really strong balance between comfort and security — they’re the goldilocks of headphones, if you will. There’s enough clamping power to prevent excess sound seeping in and keep them on your head during a workout or similar, but I never found this to be overbearing. Even when I was wearing a hat, the Ace Ultra felt really snug, with the plush ear cups and padded headband helping me to enjoy my music for many hours on end.
One subtle thing I like is how the inside of the right ear cup is green, making it easy to know which side is which when throwing the cans on. The right cup also features a slider, which can be used to easily adjust volume or trigger the Audio Swap feature. I usually prefer touch controls, but the tactile and reliable nature of these buttons might just have converted me.
Something that may frustrated a few users is that the Ace Ultra are not foldable. Yes, the ear cups rotate flat for when you want to stow the headphones in the case, but rivals like the Sony WH-1000XM6 offer a more compact, travel-friendly design. In addition, the case itself doesn’t quite offer the quality I was expecting, with a fuzzy exterior that’s a bit prone to picking up fibers. I also found that the zip jammed a bit easily. I much prefer the magnetic case of the XM6, which is more seamless to use and has a more quality look and feel.
- Design score: 4.5/5
Sonos Ace Ultra review: value
- More fully featured and better sounding than the original Ace…
- …but for the same price (at the point of launch)
- A worthwhile choice for those with or without a pre-existing Sonos system
The Sonos Ace Ultra cured the single ailment that plagued the original model above else: their middling musicality. When I tested both headphones side by side, the difference was night and day. The original Ace were held back by a limited soundstage, underwhelming instrument separation, and a lack of balance across the frequency range. But the Ace Ultra sound so much more open, organized, and detailed, and truly compete with flagship rivals from Sony and Bose.
On top of that, you’re getting excellent Dolby Atmos performance, Headphone Linking and TV Audio Swap for linking up to other Sonos products, a beautiful design, and strong noise-cancelling capabilities. Considering that the Sonos Ace Ultra cost the same as the original model did at the point of launch — and less than the standard Ace initially cost in the UK — that’s pretty impressive.
At $449 / £399 / AU$699, they’re still quite the investment, of course. And I do think that some rivals, including the Sony WH-1000XM6 and Bowers & Wilkins Px7 S3 just edge above them in terms of sound quality. But those models can’t compete when it comes to movies — a big selling point of the Ace headphones. And the interactivity that these have with other Sonos products makes them a slam-dunk for owners of products like the Sonos Beam Ultra and Sonos Play.
Even if you don’t have a Sonos system, these headphones still justify their price with great all-round performance, a delicious design, higher-res audio codecs and wired lossless sound, as well as solid battery life. All in all, then, the Ace Ultra feel like a much more worthwhile investment than the original Ace, and manage to earn their price.
- Value score: 4.5/5
Should I buy the Sonos Ace Ultra?
| Attribute | Notes | Score | 
|---|---|---|
| Features | Enhanced ANC, call quality, and battery life, better EQ options, and neat smart features like Headphone Linking. | 5/5 | 
| Sound quality | Much better musicality than the original Ace and fantastic Dolby Atmos for movies. | 4.5/5 | 
| Design | Gorgeous looks, comfortable and secure fit, but the carry case could be better. | 4.5/5 | 
| Value | Earn their price much more than the original Ace with great performance across the board. | 4.5/5 | 
Buy them if…
You want amazing headphones for movies
With Dolby Atmos compatibility and serious spatial audio skills, the Sonos Ace Ultra are arguably the best wireless headphones you can buy for movie-watching. You’ll experience expansive, three-dimensional sound with the Ace Ultra, and head-tracking will only further your immersion in any on-screen action.
You already own a Sonos system
If you own Sonos products like the Sonos Beam Gen 2 or Sonos Play, then the Ace Ultra are a very sensible buy. TV Audio Swap and Headphone Linking enable you to seamlessly transfer sound across your system, giving you unrivalled control over your music-listening and movie-viewing experiences.
Don’t buy them if…
You want the best-sounding headphones in this price-bracket
While the Sonos Ace Ultra offer great musicality, they can still be beaten. The Sony WH-1000XM6 provide a bit more bite and detailing, while the Bowers & Wilkins Px7 S3 provide even more nuanced soundstaging and instrument separation.
You want the best possible cans for travel
The Sonos Ace Ultra supply awesome ANC and do come with a carry case, but unlike some rivals, they’re not fully foldable. Rivals like the WH-1000XM6 are much more compact if you’re on the go and don’t have much space in your bag, for instance.
Sonos Ace Ultra review: also consider
| Header Cell - Column 0 | Sonos Ace Ultra | Sony WH-1000XM6 | Bowers & Wilkins Px7 S3 | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Price | $449 / £399 / AU$699 | $449 / £399 / AU$699 | $479 / £399 / AU$699 | 
| Drivers | Next-gen 40mm custom | 30mm dynamic | 40mm dynamic | 
| Active noise cancellation | Yes | Yes | Yes | 
| Battery life | 35 hours (ANC on) | 30 hours (ANC on) | 30 hours (ANC on) | 
| Weight | 0.7lbs / 322g | 0.6lbs / 254g | 0.7lbs / 300g | 
| Connectivity | Bluetooth 6.0, USB-C | Bluetooth 5.3, 3.5mm | Bluetooth 5.3, USB-C | 
| Frequency range | 20Hz-20kHz | 20Hz-20kHz | 10Hz-22kHz | 
Sony WH-1000XM6
The Sony WH-1000XM6 are true all-rounders, boasting some of the best ANC in the game, beautifully balanced audio, and a huge range of features. They’re fully foldable, offer exceptional call clarity, and support the LDAC codec for higher-res Bluetooth listening. At this price-point, they still feel like the best headphones that you can buy for the money. Read my full Sony WH-1000XM6 review.
Bowers & Wilkins Px7 S3
For me, the Bowers & Wilkins Px7 S3 are probably the best-sounding headphones you can buy in this price-range, with an exceptionally spacious, nuanced soundstage, impeccable detailing right across the frequency range, but dynamic and exciting enough to keep you engaged for hours on end. They also look truly premium, supply USB-C audio passthrough, and have an excellent control app — though their ANC isn’t anything special. Read our full Bowers & Wilkins Px7 S3 review.
How I tested the Sonos Ace Ultra
- Spent about two weeks testing
- Compared to competitors and original Sonos Ace
- Predominantly streamed music over Tidal; also watched Dolby Atmos movies
I spent about two weeks testing the Sonos Ace Ultra headphones, during which time I exhausted their various features, like TV audio swap, watched a handful of movies with Dolby Atmos soundtracks, and listened to hours worth of music.
When listening to music, I predominantly streamed tunes over Tidal on my Xiaomi 17 phone, which supports aptX codecs. To start with, I sifted through the TechRadar testing playlist, but I also listened to a wide variety of tracks from my personal library. On top of this, I compared the Sonos Ace Ultra to some of their major competitors, like the Sony WH-1000XM6, as well as the original Sonos Ace.
More generally, I’ve spent years testing gadgets here at TechRadar, where I serve as a Senior Reviews Writer. I’ve tested a wide range of audio gear, including other premium headphones like the Sony 1000X The Collexion, party speakers like the Marshall Bromley 750, Dolby Atmos soundbars like the JBL Bar 1300MK2, and more.

articles.title: Memory chips are now more expensive than compute chips on a per-area basis — AI demand drives DRAM die value past leading-edge silicon
articles.text:
Memory chips are now more expensive than compute chips on a per-area basis — AI demand drives DRAM die value past leading-edge silicon
But there is a catch.
Memory prices are at record highs due to demand from the AI sector and are not going to drop any time soon. In fact, the cost of manufacturing memory chips on a per-area basis can be higher than the price of silicon processed using TSMC's N2 and N3 fabrication technologies, which are used to make compute chips, according to an observation made by Kurnal Insights. While the comparison has merit, it has an important caveat.
Based on media leaks, Kurnal from Kurnal Insights considers that a 300-mm wafer processed using TSMC's N3 technology costs $20,000, which translates to approximately $0.283 per mm² when the wafer price is divided by its area. For TSMC's N2, the analyst assumes a considerably higher wafer price of $30,000, or around $0.424/mm². These calculations are based on unofficial information and do not account for unusable wafer edges, dicing, test structures, defects, or yield, so they should be viewed as nominal wafer-area prices rather than the actual price of usable silicon.
The calculation for DRAM works differently. Kurnal assumes a DRAM price of $1.50 per Gb and then multiplies it by the bit density of different generations. At 0.219 Gb/mm², 1y DRAM works out to $0.329/mm², whereas 1z DRAM with its 0.273 Gb/mm² density reaches $0.410/mm². Finally, 1b DRAM at 0.436 Gb/mm² produces a figure of $0.654/mm², considerably higher than the nominal $0.424/mm² calculated for an N2 wafer.
There is an important distinction here. The N2 and N3 numbers represent assumed prices charged by TSMC for processing a wafer, whereas the DRAM figures represent the potential selling value of the memory contained within a square millimeter of silicon, thus illustrating how much revenue a DRAM maker can theoretically get from a given die area at the assumed memory price.
Interestingly, Kurnal Insights' $1.50/Gb assumption is almost exactly in line with the current spot price of DDR5 eTT memory. According to DRAMeXchange, 16Gb DDR5 eTT chips carried a session-average price of $24.80 on September 21, equivalent to $1.55/Gb. At that price, 1b DRAM with a density of 0.436 Gb/mm² would be valued at approximately $0.676/mm², just 3% above Kurnal's $0.654/mm² estimate.
It goes without saying that producing DDR5 memory is considerably cheaper than making logic chips using TSMC's N3 process technology. However, with DRAM in short supply, memory makers are getting considerably more money for their silicon than they did historically.
There are a few important caveats that make the comparison somewhat less straightforward. The calculations do not account for packaging costs, with logic requiring more expensive techniques. Additionally, TSMC manufactures chips on a contract basis, and the actual price of a processed wafer depends on the volumes, customer, and other commercial terms. Thus, comparing estimated TSMC wafer prices with DRAM spot prices is not exactly an apples-to-apples comparison. Even TrendForce notes that DDR5 spot procurement remains limited and transactions are sporadic, which means spot prices do not necessarily reflect the prices at which Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix sell the bulk of their DRAM.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Therefore, contract DRAM prices would provide a considerably better basis for an economically meaningful comparison. However, we do not know contract prices, and while they are clearly higher than historical memory prices, they may not be as high as spot prices. To that end, we cannot state for sure that DRAM makers get more money for their wafers than TSMC does for its logic wafers.
Follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.
Anton Shilov is a contributing writer at Tom’s Hardware. Over the past couple of decades, he has covered everything from CPUs and GPUs to supercomputers and from modern process technologies and latest fab tools to high-tech industry trends.

articles.title: Helsinki’s Verda becomes Europe’s latest unicorn after raising €164.8 million to scale its full-stack AI cloud | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Verda (formerly DataCrunch), a Helsinki-based AI infrastructure company, announced today that it has raised €164.8 million ($189 million) in fresh funding to scale its full-stack AI cloud. With this funding, the company has become Europe’s latest unicorn.
The financing includes an oversubscribed Series B led by Emergence Capital, plus additional investment. Investors participating in the financing include MUFG Innovation Partners, Supermicro, Varma Mutual Pension Insurance Company, Lifeline Ventures, 6 Degrees Capital (6DC), byFounders, Tesi (Finnish Industry Investment Ltd). A group of angel investors also participated, including Ola Tørudbakken (Meta) and Mark Saroufim (Core Auto and GPUMODE).
“AI is becoming critical infrastructure across industries, and the next few years are a pivotal window for Europe. Our north star is to build the first true tech company in Europe, with AI infrastructure as the starting foundation, and to bring down the carbon footprint of compute worldwide. We’re proud of our progress but are a long way from being done,” said Ruben Bryon, Verda’s founder and CEO.
Founded in 2020 by Bryon, Verda is a full-stack AI cloud company that claims to manage everything from physical data centres and hardware to the cloud platform and AI research. The company highlighted that its data centres in Finland run on 100% renewable energy, drawing on the Nordics’ natural advantages in clean electricity and cooling efficiency.
Last November, DataCrunch rebranded as Verda. “The name Verda is derived from the Spanish word for ‘true’ and the Esperanto word for ‘green’. The name change symbolises and reinforces our values of technological integrity and sustainable innovation,” the company mentioned.
The announcement comes after the company reached a €143.85 million ($165 million) annualised revenue run rate in July and secured a €22 million loan from the Nordic Investment Bank (NIB). In April this year, the Finnish unicorn raised nearly €102 million ($117 million) in equity funding led by Lifeline Ventures.
Last year, in September, the company raised a total of €55 million in a Series A round led by byFounders, Skaala, Varma pension fund, and Tesi. In 2024, it raised a €12 million Seed funding round. It has raised over €392.3 million ($450 million) in total funding.
“Demand for AI compute is insatiable, and the gap between demand and supply is growing. Verda is moving quickly to secure and scale capacity, with the technology, ambition, and momentum to become a defining AI infrastructure company,” said Joe Floyd, General Partner at Emergence Capital.
The company aims to use this capital to accelerate product development across all layers of its AI cloud, from compute capacity to platform services for frontier AI teams in the agentic era.
Verda also intends to invest in areas such as inference and plans to increase its compute capacity over the next year. It recently opened offices in London and San Francisco and plans to expand further across Europe, the United States, and Asia. It operates globally and employs around 250 people from over 40 nationalities.

articles.title: Galaxy Buds 4 tem funções avançadas e está 38% mais barato no Mercado Livre • Tecnoblog

Galaxy Buds 4 tem funções avançadas e está 38% mais barato no Mercado Livre
Galaxy Buds 4 suporta áudio Hi-Fi de 24 bits, assistentes de IA por comando de voz e ANC adaptativo. Fones de ouvido estão mais baratos com cupom que encerra em algumas horas
O Galaxy Buds 4 está disponível no Mercado Livre por R$ 989 no Pix com o cupom OFERTAHJ. Um dos menores preços já encontrado pela equipe do Achados. Ao aproveitar a oferta, você garante um desconto de 38% na compra em relação ao preço original de R$ 1.599.
Os fones de ouvido de última geração da Samsung combinam uma série de funcionalidades avançadas como cancelamento ativo de ruído e assistentes de IA integrados.
Um dos destaques é o cancelamento ativo de ruído adaptativo que foi aprimorado, segundo a Samsung. Por meio de reconhecimento do nível de ruído do ambiente, a função isola desde sons mais altos até ruídos de baixa frequência. Já o recurso Chamadas Ultra Nítidas foca em entregar um áudio mais limpo especialmente para ligações e chamadas de vídeo.
O Galaxy Buds 4 conta com seis microfones (sendo três de cada lado) e suporta áudio Hi-Fi de 24 bits, ou seja, preserva ao máximo as frequências originais das músicas. Equipado por áudio 360, dispensa o uso do celular para atender ou recusar chamadas, já que reconhece a intenção a partir de movimentos feitos com a cabeça.
Os assistentes de IA: Bixby, Google Gemini e Perplexity são integrados e podem ser ativados através de comandos de voz. O usuário pode pedir para as suas notificações e mensagens sejam lidas, perguntar sobre compromissos na agenda e entre outras possibilidades.
Considerando o estojo de 515 mAh, os fones de ouvido proporcionam autonomia para até 30 horas de uso. Entretanto, com o ANC ativado a promessa é de até 5 horas de reprodução contínua. Em relação a conectividade, conta com Bluetooth 6.1 e Auto Switch que facilita a alternância entre dispositivos Galaxy.
O gadget segue com o gesto de pinça e deslize para controlar volume e outras ações. Por fim, a presença da certificação IP54 adiciona resistência contra poeira e respingos d’água ou suor. Adquira até o fim do dia o Galaxy Buds 4 por R$ 989,01 no Pix com o cupom OFERTAHJ no Mercado Livre.

articles.title: IT mistake erases 11 years of viewing history for hospitals’ maternity records
articles.text:
A “human error” in the IT department led to Nottingham University Hospitals NHS Trust (NUH) losing data from maternity records over an 11-year span.
The data loss occurred on August 18, the English hospitals announced in a blog post on Monday spotted by The Register. The blog said the problem is “the result of human error” during routine technical work while “creating a copy of a radiotherapy database for reporting purposes.”
The post reads:
The process used a set of pre-written computer instructions that had previously been used for a different hospital system. A setting that should have been changed before the process was run was missed. As a result, the process was carried out on a maternity database instead of the radiotherapy database, causing the maternity records database to be overwritten.
The overwritten database held data from NUH’s previous maternity database, which included maternity records for women and babies who received care from NUH from September 2011 to November 2022.
NUH has been unable to retrieve some of the data, the blog said:
… we have not been able to restore the complete history showing who viewed maternity records during this period. As a result, in most cases, we may be unable to confirm whether a maternity record was viewed by a particular person between September 2011 and November 2022.
NUH said that it escalated the problem “within minutes of being identified” and “worked with external specialists and reviewed other sources of information to recover as much data as possible.” It was able to restore patient care-related data, including “notes, observations, test results, and other information recorded as part of a person’s care.”

articles.title: OpenAI et Anthropic lancent GPT-6 Sol et Claude Opus 5.5 le même jour, à quelques minutes d'écart
articles.text:
Comment deux entreprises qui appellent l’industrie à ralentir le rythme peuvent-ils dégainer le même jour, à quelques minutes d’écart ? OpenAI a présenté GPT-6 Sol juste après qu’Anthropic a dévoilé Claude Opus 5.5. La course aux modèles ne ralentit pas.
OpenAI affirme que GPT-6 Sol divise par deux son taux d’erreurs par rapport à GPT-5.6, la version qui le précède directement. Le modèle est aussi facturé moitié moins cher que son prédécesseur. L’entreprise insiste surtout sur cette baisse de prix.
Le rythme s’accélère nettement chez OpenAI. Quelques semaines après GPT-6 Astra, présenté comme son modèle le plus puissant, la firme enchaîne déjà avec Sol et un second modèle, GPT-6 Luna. Ce dernier vise une gamme inférieure, censée atteindre le niveau des anciens modèles haut de gamme pour un coût bien moindre. Une façon de couvrir plusieurs segments d’un coup, du modèle premium au plus abordable.
Le prix, nouveau nerf de la guerre
Ce virage vers l’accessibilité économique n’a rien d’anodin. Pendant des mois, chaque annonce se jouait sur les scores et les records de puissance. OpenAI déplace ici le terrain sur le coût d’usage, celui que paient vraiment les développeurs et les entreprises qui branchent ces modèles dans leurs produits. C’est le terrin d’affrontement avec Google et Anthropic.
En face, Anthropic a dévoilé Claude Opus 5.5 dans la même soirée du 22 septembre. Il promet là aussi des performances 40% moins cher qu’Opus 5 et un niveau comparable à Fable 5.1.
Cette quasi-simultanéité en dit long. Deux annonces à quelques minutes d’écart trahissent une veille concurrentielle menée en temps réel, où aucun ne veut laisser l’autre occuper seul l’espace médiatique. Les deux entreprises ont d’ailleurs pris l’habitude de se répondre du tac au tac : cet été, Anthropic revendiquait un test écrasé face à OpenAI, qui a repris la main en ajustant deux paramètres. La bataille des annonces prolonge celle des benchmarks.
L’ironie est difficile à ignorer. Quelques jours plus tôt, Dario Amodei demandait à l’industrie de ralentir le développement de l’IA, un appel que Sam Altman disait approuver. Pour les développeurs et les entreprises qui paient l’accès à ces modèles, la baisse des coûts est une bonne nouvelle immédiate. Sur la promesse de lever le pied, on repassera.

articles.title: Durabook Announces the Z14I-DX3 Rugged Mobile Laptop, a Triple-display, Workstation-class, Edge AI Laptop
articles.text:
Tuesday, September 22nd 2026
	
	
	
	
Durabook Announces the Z14I-DX3 Rugged Mobile Laptop, a Triple-display, Workstation-class, Edge AI Laptop
Durabook, the global rugged mobile solutions brand owned by Twinhead International Corporation, announced today the Z14I-DX3 Rugged Mobile Laptop with three full HD displays integrated in a workstation-class, edge AI computing platform. The Z14I-DX3's three 14-inch full HD displays keep maps, video, and operational data visible at the same time, providing a clear, comprehensive view of situational awareness and enabling better informed decision-making for professionals
The Z14I-DX3 workstation-class, edge AI computing platform is powered by Intel Core Ultra CPUs with an integrated Intel AI Boost NPU. A significant option for the Z14I-DX3 is a dedicated NVIDIA graphics card delivering up to 682 TOPS that enables high-end visualization performance such as real-time image recognition, sensor data fusion, and edge computing. Equipped with modern computing performance and formidable acceleration for demanding AI workloads and next-generation AI applications at the edge, the Z14I-DX3 functions as a mission command center.Designed for rapid deployment, the Z14I-DX3's integrated triple-screen configuration keeps all three displays securely attached, with the two expansion displays folding inward for compact transport and unfolding into an expansive command workspace, making it easy to move between operating locations as one integrated unit. The rugged edge laptop adheres to MIL-STD-810H and MIL-STD-461G certifications for the benefit of field professionals on defense and military deployments, in public safety and emergency services, utilities and energy industry, field engineering and industrial operations, maritime environments, and outdoor infrastructure operations.
Twinhead CEO Fred Kao"The Z14I-DX3 Rugged Mobile Laptop with its triple-screen display is a prime example of how Durabook goes beyond the expected upgrades of rugged computing technology," "The Z14I-DX3 combines the capabilities expected from a Durabook rugged computer with an expansive multi-screen workspace and AI capability in a powerful edge computing platform."
In field application the Z14I-DX3 triple-display laptop can serve as a rugged mobile command center for coordinating personnel, communications, and operational monitoring. Rather than repeatedly switching between applications on a single screen, the three-display, edge computing, AI platform enables personnel to view and work with multiple applications, UAV/drone control and telemetry data, mission maps, live video feeds, sensor or payload data, diagnostics, and other mission-critical information side by side. This visual workspace allows data processing and real-time analysis to take place closer to where operational data is generated, helping field teams turn mission data into actionable information without relying solely on cloud-based processing.Built for clear visibility in demanding outdoor environments, the Z14I-DX3 combines three 14-inch FHD 1200-nit DynaVue sunlight-readable touchscreens with capacitive multi-touch and built-in On-screen Display (OSD) controls. Touchscreen brightness can be synchronized across all displays or adjusted individually and they support Finger/Water, Glove and Stylus modes, giving field professionals flexible and reliable interaction across changing working conditions.
For high-load AI applications, the platform can be configured with an optional NVIDIA discrete GPU available as the RTX A500 AI accelerator, RTX 3500 Ada, or RTX 5000 Ada, with the RTX 5000 Ada alone delivering up to 682 TOPS of AI performance. Combined with the platform's integrated NPU and CPU, total system AI performance exceeds that TOPS number.
The Z14I-DX3 combines extensive modern and legacy connectivity to support a wide range of field communications options, peripherals and specialized equipment. Interfaces include Thunderbolt 4, dual RJ-45 Ethernet, two RS-232 serial ports, ExpressCard 54, Nano SIM and eSIM, plus USB options from USB 3.2 Gen 2 to USB 2.0 for flexible field integration. Wireless capabilities include Intel Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 5.4, with optional dedicated GPS, 4G LTE and 5G connectivity.
Advanced security features of the Z14I-DX3 include a range of multi-factor authentication options, such as a smart card reader and optional Windows Hello webcam, RFID/NFC reader and fingerprint scanner. The system includes dual removable quick-release NVMe PCIe SSD drives, allowing users to swap storage drives within seconds without tools for operational continuity in mission-critical environments.
The new Z14I-DX3 Rugged Mobile Laptop is available for purchase now.

articles.title: Das Erdsystem gerät zunehmend aus dem Gleichgewicht
articles.text:
Planetare Belastungsgrenzen: Nur 2 von 9 Umwelt-Indikatoren im grünen Bereich – und es wird schlimmer
Der Planetary Health Check soll einen jährlichen Überblick über den Zustand der Erde geben. Forscher:innen des Potsdam-Instituts für Klimafolgenforschung (Pik) nehmen dabei neun sogenannte planetare Belastungsgrenzen unter die Lupe. Darunter versteht man miteinander verbundene Erdsystem-Prozesse. Diese müssen sich den Forscher:innen zufolge innerhalb sicherer Grenzen bewegen, um Stabilität und Widerstandsfähigkeit unseres Planeten zu erhalten.
Planetare Belastungsgrenzen unter Druck
Dem aktuellen Gesundheitscheck der Erde zufolge befinden sich allerdings schon sieben dieser neun Indikatoren außerhalb des sicheren Bereichs. Alle sieben betroffenen Grenzen sind mittlerweile so stark überschritten wie nie zuvor, wie es in einer PIK-Mitteilung heißt.
Bei den planetaren Belastungsgrenzen, die schon außerhalb des sicheren Handlungsspielraums liegen, handelt es sich um: Klimawandel, Integrität der Biosphäre, Veränderung der Landnutzung, Veränderung des Süßwasserkreislaufs, Veränderung der biogeochemischen Kreisläufe, Eintrag menschengemachter Substanzen und Ozeanversauerung. Den Forscher:innen zufolge haben sich in den vergangenen zehn Jahren lediglich die Werte in puncto Ozonschicht und globale Aerosolbelastung der Atmosphäre verbessert.
Risiko unumkehrbarer Veränderungen steigt
Insgesamt steige damit das Risiko „großräumiger, langfristiger und potenziell unumkehrbarer Veränderungen“, wie Boris Sakschewski, PIK-Forscher und Leitautor des Berichts, warnt. „Gleichzeitig wird unser Spielraum, diesen Problemen wirksam zu begegnen, immer kleiner“, so Sakschewski.
Allerdings gibt es noch Hoffnung, wie PIK-Direktor Johan Rockström ergänzt: „Wir wissen, was zu tun ist, und haben die Möglichkeiten und Lösungen, um gegenzusteuern.“ Allerdings sei es wichtig, jetzt schnell zu handeln. „Nur so können wir unser Leben und unsere Lebensgrundlagen schützen und Wohlstand für alle auch in Zukunft sichern“, wie Rockström erklärt.
Das System gerät jedenfalls zunehmend aus dem Gleichgewicht. Hitzewellen, Dürren, Starkregen, Rekordtemperaturen in Ozeanen oder extreme Kälteeinbrüche zählen laut den Forscher:innen zu den „Überlastungssymptomen“. Klimaforscherin Levke Caesar vergleicht dies mit einem „angeschlagenen Immunsystem“, aufgrund dessen man häufiger krank wird.
Kohlenstoffsenken: CO₂‑Aufnahme gefährdet
Insbesondere im Blick hat der Planetary Health Check 2026 die sogenannten Kohlenstoffsenken, Vegetation und Böden, die einen großen Teil der vom Menschen verursachten CO₂‑Emissionen aufnehmen. Hitze, Dürre und Brände sowie die Schädigung von Ökosystemen können diese CO₂‑Aufnahme verringern, wie die Forscher:innen warnen.
In der Folge könnten sich einige CO₂‑Senken zu CO₂‑Quellen entwickeln. Die Beobachtungen seien „ein Warnsignal dafür, dass unser Planet möglicherweise einen Teil seiner Fähigkeit verliert, die zunehmenden, von uns verursachten Belastungen abzupuffern“, wie Studienautor Sakschewski betont.

articles.title: The Beats 360 are fun headphones that you can mix and match
articles.text:
For the past couple of weeks, I’ve been using the Beats 360 for my flights and commutes, and I’m impressed by Beats’ newest and flashiest headphones ever.
The audio device is made to be used all the time, whether you’re at the gym or you’re out and about looking fancy. I really appreciate the customizable headphones; you’re able to swap out ear cups and headband cushion, so you can mix and match to your liking.
At first, I was a bit skeptical because I thought swapping would be a pain in the ass. In the past, when companies say that something is easy to swap out, I’ve found it usually isn’t quite so easy. But what I like about the Beats 360 is that they’re kind of idiot proof, and this is what I need: idiot-proof customization options, and I’m pleased.
With a twist, the cups pop off the headphones, and another twist helps you put new colours in. At the top, the headband has little holes on the underside that make it easy to clip the cushion into it. They’re so easy to remove that another tech creator just snatched an earcup when I was wearing the headphones around my neck.
Now, swappable cups alone wouldn’t be exciting, except Beats lets you mix and match colours, and that’s pretty dope. The headphones come in Black, Cloud, Sky and Pink, and of course these all have matching pieces, but there’s also ‘Spark,’ which is like a neon yellow, and Navy, giving you tons of colours to mix and match. There are also leather options in Black and Cloud as well for a night out on the town. My favourite combination is the Black headset with Spark.
The Beats 360 are IPX4 and come with ‘Performance Knit’ cups that allow you to sweat in the earbuds without damaging them. And if your workout is intense, you can easily swap out the cups or the headband cushion. I’m a pretty sweaty dude, so I was able to see that the cups dealt pretty well with sweat.
The Beats 360 feel okay on your head. They’re comfortable after you start wearing them for a while. At least I found the top band a bit tight on my head, but after wearing them for 20 minutes, this feeling goes away. The Performance Knit cushions also use plush memory foam, which might explain why it starts to feel better after some time. Maybe the shape of my head is weird because I found the AirPods Max headphones more comfortable, which people tend to complain about. But the degree of comfort isn’t that bad at all. For instance, I wore them on a seven-hour flight straight, and even fell asleep while wearing them.
The Beats 360 sound great; Beats said they improved the active noise cancellation from the Beats Studio. It’s pretty good at shutting out most noise without needing to raise the volume too loud. Airplane and subway sounds disappear completely; however, the high-pitched sound of a baby crying made it through. The baby was an aisle over on a two-aisle plane, but it wasn’t like I could 100 per cent tell what I was hearing at first. I just thought it was a sound in the background of my show. I was watching Secret Lives of Mormon Wives; all these women have babies, but when I removed the headphones, it was like, “Oh, this baby isn’t on my show, and is pretty loud.”
The Beats 360 offers rich sound with immersive audio. I played music and watched media for hours, and it all sounds great. It also has Adaptive EQ, which adjusts acoustic frequencies based on the fit. Plus, there’s Personalized Spatial Audio with head tracking and Dolby Atmos, with a built-in accelerometer and gyroscope for head tracking.
When I was testing audio, I picked songs like Middle Child by J.Cole, Another One Bites the Dust by Queen, Humble by Kendrick Lamar, and We Are Young, which are pretty different songs, but also the same ones I used to test Apple’s AirPods Max 2. It’s pretty interesting comparing the two headphones; both sound good and are immersive. Strangely, I think the Beats 360 are even louder than the AirPods Max 2, but loudness isn’t everything.
I found that Middle Child had a bit of a punch to the bass that was a little bit overwhelming (though I was playing the music at the loudest volume to compare), which isn’t something I hear with the AirPods Max 2. Other songs like Another One Bites the Dust and Humble sounded very similar on the two headsets; voices are clear and precise, so you can hear harmonies very well. For instance, there’s a very quiet harmony in We Are Young that’s slightly delayed, like an echo, that I can hear pretty well between both headsets.
However, the experience between the two headphones for We Are Young is interesting. I think the instrumentals are stronger on the AirPods Max 2, as it feels like We Are Young is a huge production, whereas on the Beats 360, you can hear a lot, but it sounds a bit lacking. But again, I definitely needed to keep the volume on max to hear the difference.
One thing I found a little weird: when you take off the headphones, your media doesn’t auto-pause. Also, the Beats 360 work on both Android and iOS, but you need to download the Beats app on Android, while on iOS, it just works and you can control the headphones via your settings, similar to any AirPods.
I enjoyed the Beats 360 headphones, but definitely my favourite thing was the customizable cushions and the variety of colours they come in. Although I noted that there weren’t any red options, which feels like a miss considering it’s Beats. The Beats 360 costs $479.95, and the cushion kit costs $74.95. However, until October 31, you can grab different cushion kits for $14.99, which I think is a sick introductory offer that I might take advantage of — I love mixing and matching.

articles.title: Anthropic lanza Claude Opus 5.5: su IA más segura y barata hasta ahora
articles.text:
A unos días de pedir una pausa en el desarrollo de la IA, Anthropic anunció Claude Opus 5.5, uno de sus modelos más poderosos. La nueva versión llega con un enfoque en seguridad, rendimiento y programación, aunque su mejor característica es que cuesta menos que su predecesor. De acuerdo con Anthropic, este es el primer modelo evaluado bajo el nuevo estándar de cautela que pide la industria.
En términos prácticos, Claude Opus 5.5 es un modelo más rápido, barato y seguro cuando se compara con Opus 5. Anthropic afirma que su nueva IA consiguió completar un proyecto de migración con 680.000 líneas de código en menos de un día, algo que a un equipo de ingenieros le habría tomado semanas. Opus 5.5 requiere menos cálculos que el modelo anterior, por lo que los usuarios se ahorrarían hasta un 40% en cargas de trabajo típicas.
La parte más importante del anuncio tiene que ver con la seguridad. Anthropic, al igual que OpenAI, Microsoft y otros laboratorios de IA, han empujado el discurso apocalíptico durante las últimas semanas. El hackeo de Hugging Face por parte de agentes autónomos de OpenAI desató una oleada de temores y críticas hacia los sistemas de seguridad que tienen estos modelos. Sobre esta línea, Anthropic dice que Claude Opus 5.5 consigue las mejores puntuaciones de seguridad y es menos probable que se salga de control.
Antes de su lanzamiento, la compañía sometió el modelo a evaluadores externos como Frontier Design y METR. En la prueba de alineamiento más exhaustiva que aplica la empresa, Opus 5.5 es el modelo con mejor desempeño. Anthropic dice que tiene mucha menor tendencia a tomar acciones difíciles de revertir o a actuar fuera de los límites que se le establecen. Esta versión resiste mejor los intentos de prompt injection, en donde los hackers escriben instrucciones maliciosas para manipular el comportamiento de la IA.
Claude Opus 5.5 da un salto notable en rendimiento y desarrollo de software
Más allá de la seguridad, Claude Opus 5.5 es una bala en cuanto a rendimiento. Según las primeras pruebas, el modelo puede completar trabajos complejos en menor tiempo y detectar ineficiencias. En un test interno en donde se le pidió reducir los tiempos de carga en todas las páginas de una aplicación web, Opus 5.5 tuvo éxito en 39 de los 40 intentos sin alterar el comportamiento de la aplicación.
En el caso de trabajos de análisis y redacción de informes, Claude pudo elaborar un reporte sobre los resultados trimestrales de una empresa usando fuentes difíciles de localizar. Un evaluador verificó cada dato y cita contra las fuentes originales y encontró que Opus 5.5 superó el estándar de calidad exigido en 16 de 18 intentos. Esta versión superó a Opus 5 y Fable 5.1, quienes no consiguieron alcanzar la marca requerida en ningún intento.
Pasando al desarrollo de software, Claude Opus 5.5 demostró su utilidad en tareas como auditorías y migraciones de bases de código completas. Un usuario auditó y corrigió una base de 200.000 líneas en menos de tres horas, frente a las más de 20 horas que le tomó a Claude Opus 5, usando 2,5 veces más poder de procesamiento. En otra prueba, Anthropic le pidió traducir la herramienta HAProxy del lenguaje C a Rust, la cual completó en 9,5 horas y con un 51% menos de recursos que Fable 5.1.
Siguiendo en este terreno, Anthropic añadió capas de protección adicionales a los agentes. Ahora contarán con un clasificador que revisa cada acción antes de ejecutarla, un entorno aislado que puede ser auditado por un equipo de seguridad, así como también una revisión automática que detecta vulnerabilidades. En teoría, las empresas que dejan a estos agentes operar de forma autónoma durante largos períodos ya no tendrán que preocuparse de su seguridad.
Claude Opus 5.5 ya está disponible en la web, aplicación móvil y el resto de plataformas de desarrollo, entre las que se incluyen Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud y Microsoft Azure. El modo rápido para Opus 5.5 también está disponible en Claude Code y la API y tiene un coste de 0,2 dólares por millón de tokens en lecturas de caché.

articles.title: GPT-6 Astra Breaks an Old Enigma Message - Schneier on Security
articles.text:
GPT-6 Astra Breaks an Old Enigma Message
This is pretty amazing:
However, the most astonishing thing about this break is that the GPT6 Astra did it entirely on its own. Carter Leffer only directed GPT6 Astra to see if it could break any of the unbroken Enigma messages published on the Crypto Cellar Research web page. After analysing the unbroken messages on the website, it decided that the most promising message was Nr. 172, MVUEH and it also quickly suspected that the plaintext of Nr. 173, SIPVX, might be related to the plaintext of the unbroken MVUEH message. After trying many different approaches, GPT6 Astra focused on using the repeated place name ROSENOW ROSENOW as a crib. After developing the necessary Python and C++ software for an Enigma simulator and an Enigma Bombe, GPT6 Astra started a thorough break with the ROSENOW crib, which in the end resulted in the correct key and plaintext for the MVUEH message being found.
We are still analysing the GPT6 Astra logs to see exactly how it executed the break. And we are discovering amazing details.
More details at the link.
Michael Donnelly • September 22, 2026 9:47 AM
“The file references GPT–6 Astra mentions…are correct, but they are not available on the Crypto Cellar Research website. GPT–6 Astra mentions a private collection, but it is not clear what this is, whether it has succeeded in accessing the Bundesarchiv’s digitised collections or whether it has found these files elsewhere.”
How is it that they can’t figure out where it got the file references? That seems like something that would be in the logs. At least the Bundesarchiv’s digitised collections, so accessing them there wouldn’t involve hacking into anything.

articles.title: OpenAI launches GPT-6 Sol and Luna, boasting lower cost and fewer mistakes | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Earlier this month, OpenAI launched GPT-6 Astra, which it heralded as its most powerful and capable model yet, and the “world’s best model” for a variety of activities, including computer work and coding. Now, the lab is expanding the GPT-6 generation with updated versions of the smaller Sol and Luna models.
“GPT-6 Astra introduced a new generation of intelligence; these models extend its benefits by making that intelligence more efficient and accessible,” the company writes.
The first models in the Sol and Luna series were introduced earlier this year, representing different tiers in OpenAI’s hierarchy of models. Sol is designed for complex tasks like coding, while OpenAI says Luna is more appropriate for clerical work — “high-volume tasks with a clear goal, like summarizing documents, extracting information, or answering quick questions.”
OpenAI is also emphasizing big improvements in efficiency and affordability — most notably, via a substantial price drop for API access. The 6 series models will be available at half the cost of the 5.6 series of Sol and Luna, a price drop that OpenAI attributes to improvements in caching and inference.
OpenAI also claims that its newest models are better at producing answers that are factually accurate, and notes that they have a lower error rate when it comes to coding.
“On our internal factuality evaluation, which is based on de-identified real-world conversations where users flagged mistakes by our models, GPT-6 Sol makes about half as many mistakes as its predecessor, reaching Astra-level reliability at much lower cost,” the announcement reads.
As is typical with OpenAI’s new model releases, the company is claiming that its newest offerings outshine those of its primary competitor, Anthropic. The company repeatedly claims that GPT-6 Sol and Luna handle tasks substantially better than Anthropic’s top models — like Fable and Opus.
Notably, Anthropic released a new version of Opus 5.5 just 90 minutes before OpenAI’s release, reflecting the intense competition between the two companies.
The new versions of Sol and Luna are now available in ChatGPT Work and Codex for most paid accounts, and in the ChatGPT API, while Luna will be available in the desktop app and for Free and Go users. OpenAI expects to roll out the models to ChatGPT (the app and website) gradually throughout the day.

articles.title: Vast Data launches confidential computing service for sensitive workloads - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Vast Data launches confidential computing service for sensitive workloads
Vast Data Inc. today introduced DataEnclave, a confidential computing environment designed to let companies run advanced artificial intelligence models against sensitive data without exposing either the data or the model’s intellectual property.
DataEnclave is a new capability within the Vast DataEngine and broader Vast AI Operating System that uses Nvidia Corp.’s confidential computing technology to create hardware-isolated environments in which proprietary models and enterprise data can be decrypted and processed securely.
The technology targets financial institutions, healthcare providers, government agencies and other organizations that cannot move regulated or sensitive information to externally hosted AI services. It also addresses model developers’ reluctance to distribute proprietary model weights into infrastructure they do not control.
“Model weights are fast becoming the most valuable intellectual property in the world,” said Jeff Denworth (pictured), Vast Data’s co-founder. “Base weights define the value of frontier models, while fine-tuned weights will increasingly represent the proprietary intelligence of AI-driven enterprises.”
DataEnclave uses trusted execution environments spanning central processing units and graphics processing units. It encrypts guest memory, graphics processing unit memory and NVLink traffic while isolating active models and data from administrators, infrastructure operators and other tenants.
A cryptographic attestation process verifies the hardware, software and governing policies before models or data are decrypted. Enterprises and model developers retain control of their respective encryption keys through integrations with their own key management systems.
“Up until now, there hasn’t been a great solution for ensuring that the memory space that people do this computing in is equally protected,” Denworth said. “Once you get to the final computing destination, is that environment safe enough to actually decrypt the world’s most sensitive data?”
Flexible deployment
DataEnclave can be deployed in customer data centers, AI clouds and fully air-gapped environments. Its attestation services are based on the open-source Cloud Native Computing Foundation Trustee project or can be provided through Fortanix Inc.’s Confidential AI offering.
The system also logs attestation events, key releases and enclave lifecycle activity in the Vast DataBase data warehouse. These records provide an audit trail showing which workloads ran and under what policies without revealing the protected data or model weights.
Initial model and software partners include Cohere Inc., CrowdStrike Holdings Inc., Deepgram Inc., The San Francisco AI Factory Inc., Fundamental Research Labs Inc. and TwelveLabs Inc. Cisco Systems Inc. and Super Micro Computer Inc. are among the hardware partners that will offer integrated systems.
Vast said the model allows a developer’s base weights and a customer’s fine-tuned weights to operate together while remaining under separate ownership and key control. That could help enterprises create customized models without disclosing their proprietary training or operational data to the base-model provider.
“Both of those can interoperate within this multitenant enclave where we can support the trust requirements of both organizations simultaneously,” Denworth said.
Vast is initially concentrating on organizations with particularly strict security and data residency requirements. Denworth identified large banks, intelligence and defense agencies and pharmaceutical companies as early target customers.
“In all three cases, they have said that this solves major pains for them in that they’re not allowed to send certain data products up to different services that they want to use,” he said. “It’s basically the most regulated and air-gapped customers of the world.”
The company also argues that DataEnclave could change the economics of enterprise AI. Customers could run proprietary models on infrastructure they own or select a regional AI cloud, reducing model developers’ need to finance the underlying computing capacity.
For Vast, the capability will be included in the existing AI Operating System rather than sold as a separate product. “We don’t charge anything extra for this,” Denworth said. “It’s just part of the AI operating system stack.”
DataEnclave is available in preview and is scheduled to ship in the first quarter of 2027 through Vast and participating hardware partners, including Cisco and Supermicro.
